Oil motion of Hon. P. E. Blondin (Minister of Inland Revenue), Bill No. 115, to amend the Inland Revenue Act, was read the second time, considered in Committee, reported, Tead the third time, and passed.
[Mr. Sam. Hughes.J

On motion of Hon. P. E. Blondin (Minister of Inland Revenue), the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Minister of Inland Revenue may authorize the employment of such temporary or acting officers of Excise in the second or outside division of the Department of Inland Revenue as are required to carry on the work of the department, that no such officer shall receive a higher salary than the salary allowed to permanent officers of the same rank and class, and no such salary shall be paid until voted by Parliament.
Are these officers to do the ordinary work of the department or some new work?

This amendment is in order to include in the Inland Revenue Act a clause similar to clause 6 of the Customs Act, regarding the appointment of temporary officials by Order in Council. In the past, and I am referring now to both the late Administration and the present, temporary officers were appointed by the Minister of Inland Revenue, under the impression that Clause 6 of the Customs Act also applied to InlandRevenue appointments. The attention of the department has been drawn to it by the Auditor General, and this is only to give authority to the department for what has been done in the past. It does not refer at all to any new employees; it refers only to the general employees, with whom the department is without power to-day to deal, and to the payment of whom the Auditor General would object in the future if this amendment were not provided.

I would be afraid that the minister proposed to appoint an army of employees. A few days ago, when discussing his Estimates, he said that he in- . tended to appoint some new employees to prevent the adulteration of maple syrup and sugar. I thought that perhaps this legislation was to provide for the appointment of these new employees.

Not at all. As for the Bill passed yesterday, I think .1 gave a satisfactory explanation, I believe that both sides of the House were anxious that I should appoint as many employees as are necessary to see that the law is complied with.

If I und .rstand the resolution properly, it is simply

to change the mode of appointing officers. Do I understand that officers are now appointed by Order in Council and that the object is to have them appointed by the minister?

No. We have to employ temporary officers in the Inland Revenue Department just as they have to do in the Customs Department. If we need additional help we have to employ temporary officers, some for a month or two, or perhaps some for a year. Most of the officers appointed by the department have to be appointed temporarily in order that they may become used to the service, and after a time, if they prove themselves competent, they are appointed permanently. It was found by the Auditor General that under the present law we had no authority to employ temporary hands. That is the reason of the amendment.
I understood that the object was to have in the Inland Revenue Department the same law as prevails in the Customs Department. What is the law governing the Customs Department?	_

We have no authority
to make these appointments, although they have foeen made by the minister in the past. Section 6 of the Customs Act provides that:
The minister may, from time to time, authorize the employment of such temporary or acting officers of custom in the second or outside division of the Department of Customs as are required to carry on the work of the department.
2. No such officer so employed shall receive a higher salary than he would be allowed if appointed permanently to the same rank and class ; nor shall any such salary be paid until voted by Parliament.

Then what
you are proposing is the same as this?
Yes.
Will that indude temporary clerks appointed at Ottawa?
No, it only applies to temporary employees in the outside service.
Are there many temporary employees in the department?
There are not more than the usual number. I understand that there are between 200 and 300 temporary employees all over the Dominion.

Are they employed all
the year round or only for a few months?
It depends on their employment. Most of them are employed all the year round.
What particular work are these temporary employees put at?

They are employed in
the different offices all over the country.
At what particular work?

The usual work. As I explained a few moments ago, when at Montreal, Quebec or elsewhere, we take on new employees we always-take them on temporarily,' and after a while they may be appointed permanently.
Do I understand the minister to say that this is only the opening wedge to 'make men permanent? You say he employs them temporarily and then they are made permanent?

No; that is not what I mean. Some of them, if their services are required and if they have been found duly qualified, will be appointed permanently. My hon. friend will understand that it is a great advantage to put a man on and test him before appointing him permanently.

Does this amendment
give the minister a means of evading the Civil Service Act?

It only applies to the
outside service. What we are asking Parliament to do is only to give the Inland Revenue Department the same right as it gave to the Customs Department. Clause 6 exists for the Customs Department but it does not exist for the Inland Revenue Department. In the past, the late Government appointed temporarily officials without any authority and it is to correct this condition that we are bringing in this legislation.
Then these employees will not have to obtain a certificate from the Civil Service Commission?
They never have to in the outside service.
Has the Auditor General paid these men up to the present?
Yes.
What causes the question to arise now? Is it owing to the great number of men recently employed?
I suppose some lawyer in the department has raised the question and it has been brought to my attention.

The Department of the Auditor General is a progressive department, but it does not pretend to know everything all at once. It finds out that it has been making payments without proper authorization. It does not want to do wrong any more and it asks you to put it in a position to do right.
I notice that the Auditor General's Department has been progressing very well lately.

Do as we do-turn
'them out when they do wrong.

In what particular
branch of the outside service are these employees required-weights and measures, gas and electricity inspection, selling stamps, or where?

In every branch, mostly in the Excise Department.
Mr. MARCH.: Is there any age limit for appointment to the outside service in the Inland Revenue Department?
No.
You can appoint them as old as you like?
They appointed one 87 years old in Three Rivers.

You appointed
one after he was dead.
You let them vote after they are dead.

When you appoint a man to the outside service do you require that he should qualify or pass an examination for the work that he is to do before you appoint him, or do you appoint him subject to the examination being passed later on?
We appoint him subject to examination. We can appoint a man . temporarily without an examination but in order to be permanent he has to undei'go examination.
Do you allow him a certain time in which to qualify for his work?
No. It all depends on the necessity of making a new permanent appointment for the work that is being done in his locality.

When you appoint a man and he turns out to be incompetent for the work for which he is appointed, do you

keep him on or do you give him a specified time in which he must pass an examination to show his .qualification for the work?

When we want to make a new permanent appointment, the man is advised that he will have a certain time in which to pass his examination. If his services are not found to be satisfactory, all the department has to do is to turn him out.

In my constituency we have two employees in the Weights and Measures Branch. One ceased to be an employee, having been dismissed for political partisanship, and he has since become a member of the Quebec Legislature. The other was dismissed on the same ground after an investigation which lasted a couple of years. Three men were appointed to fill their places: one from Gaspe, Mr. Myles; one from Bonaventure, Mr. Dag-neau; and one from Rimouski, Mr. Desjardins. Have those three men qualified for the work for which they were appointed, and are they still in the service of the department?
They are still in the service of the department; they have not yet qualified for permanent positions.
Why was it necessary to appoint three men to fill two vacancies?
Was the change made by me?
No, it was made by your predecessor.
Would my hon. friend object to my taking some more time to look into the matter?
Certainly not.

Appointments under
this proposed legislation are undesirable, because it seems to enlarge the scope of appointments that are not under the guardianship of the Civil Service Commission. The whole trend of better public opinion at present is in the way of revolt against patronage. I say this without a partisan meaning, because both sides may more or less have erred in that regard. What rule does the minister apply to .men who are taken on, and who have not over them the guardianship of the commission, in the way of protecting the country against partisans? The other day he laid it down as a principle that the gentleman next to him in position might indulge in free speech, and perhaps become offensive to

18TI
45 per cent of the people of Canada, by his abusive utterances against one of the great parties in Canada, but that the minister would in no way interfere with his freedom of speech. I am not going to revive the discussion in reference to the deputy minister, who was the subject of discussion; but as regards those men who are appointed entirely from political recommendations and who are not under the control of the commission, what is the minister's policy with regard to their indulging in controversial partisan disputes in the country, either at election time or at any other time?
They.have no right whatever to take an active part in politics. If any one of my officials should persist in such a course, I would have to dismiss him.

Would the minister
apply that principle to his deputy minister?
That is another question which I would ask my hon. friend not to bring up on this resolution.

One of the difficulties in the making of those temporary appointments is that a great'number of officials are called temporary when they really are permanent-,- although, legally speaking, they are only temporary, because they have never been appointed to permanent positions. As soon as a Government changes, no matter what Government it is, pressure is brought to bear upon it to dispense with the services of such men, and it is said: why, such a man is only a temporary employee anyway; he has not a permanent position. Although he may have worked for ten years in the Government service he is still considered as a temporary employee. There ought to be some change in that respect. When a man or a woman has been in the employ of the Government for a certain length of time, that employee ought to become what is called permanent, so that dismissal could not occur without ail Order in Council and without cause. Hundreds of so-called temporary employees are really permanent, although they are called temporary and subject to dismissal for reasons which do not apply to permanent employees. The Department of Customs, the Post Office Department and the Department of Inland Revenue are the departments that have the greatest number of temporary employees while .the Department of Interior has also a great many. Such people may be employed for six weeks or for six years; but
they have no protection against dismissal although they may be the best employees in in the Government.

I should like to emphasize the remarks of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). There is a very singular case in Peterborough that illustrates the importance of what my hon. friend says. A fine old gentleman was appointed by the late Government to a position in Peterborough on the temporary list. That man cannot be turned out. He is over eighty years of age. He is ageing and he raises Cain with the customers. Application has been made by the collector to have him dismissed, but I said that I would not consent to have him dismissed. He comes of an excellent family that has survived the evils of Liberalism. The fact of the matter is that the man, if he were dismissed to-morrow, would be out on the street. He has been for many years in the service. If automatically he could have become a permanent clerk, he would be entitled to a retiring allowance; but as it is, he is not. It is impossible in the name of humanity to let that man go, but what are we to do? Is there no remedy for that sort of thing?

Let us say that two men who are appointed under this proposed legislation show political partisanship and one of them displays partisanship in favour of the present Government, and the other in favour of the Liberals. 'Will the minister always use the two of them alike, and always adopt the policy that he has just annunciated? Will he fire a Tory for as little partisanship as he will a Grit?

The minister is bound
to follow the same line of policy towards all employees.
Will he do it?~
Certainly.

Has the minister under
this proposed legislation power tq appoint any of these officers in the city of Hull, which adjoins Ottawa, but which is in another province?
We have no other object in proposing this amendment than to correct an irregular procedure under the law.
But the minister will have power to appoint Excise and Inland Revenue officers in the city of Hull under this legislation when it is passed?
I am not informed that there is any necessity for such appointments.

The city of Hull has over 20,000 population. It is true, it borders on the city of Ottawa, but it is divided from Ottawa by the Ottawa river. The minister can see the city of Hull even as he looks from Parliament Hill. It is a very important commercial city, perhaps the greatest manufacturing city along certain lines in the Dominion of Canada. It would be a great convenience to the city of Hull to have these officers appointed. Just prior to going out of power the late Government opened a customs office in Hull, and that office yields great profit to the Government' >and is of immense advantage to the surrounding section of country. This proposed law will give the Minister of Inland Bevenue power to appoint similar officers for his department in the city of Hull, and I ask him if he will not appoint some of these officers for the good of the public service and the general convenience of the people?
I will give the remarks of my hon. friend all consideration, and if there is necessity I will make the appointments.
I am a little surprised at my hon. friend from' Wright (Mr. Devlin).
Surprised?

Yes, that he would put temptation in the way of the Minister of Inland Revenue and urge it upon him. The minister's answer was that if there were no necessity there would he no appointments. Now the hon. gentleman is trying to induce the minister to appoint officers in Hull simply because Hull can be seen from Ottawa and is the largest manufacturing city in the world. Surely he cannot wish officers appointed, even in Hull, if there is no necessity for them.
Perhaps my language was not clear to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I was speaking non-politically.
As usual.

I try to speak nonpolitically. I was pointing out the importance of the city of Hull and its peculiar situation. Although it is near the city of Ottawa it serves a portion of the country which cannot 'be conveniently served by the 
officers in Ottawa city. There was formerly necessity for opening a customs office there, and there is the same necessity for opening an Inland Revenue office. I would not ask the Government to spend a dollar where there is no necessity. 1 am only sorry the Government is in the habit of spending money where there is no necessity.
I do not understand this measure. Does it mean that the minister is getting power to pay yearly salaries to men who are employed only a few months in the year?

No, I am only asking
that a privilege enjoyed by every other department of the Government should be extended to the Department of Inland Revenue.

The resolution says: "No such officer shall receive a higher salary than the salary paid to permanent officers of the same rank and class." Would not that put them in the same rank as the permanent employees?
No. It means that they cannot be appointed at a higher salary than that of the permanent officers whom they may be called upon to replace temporarily.
But if the minister already has the power to employ temporary employees what does he need this for?

I have not the power,
while other departments have.

Does this give the
minister any power that he has not previously exercised? I understand not.

Up to this time certain appointments have been made, but the Auditor General has notified the minister and the department that this is not legal and that he cannot any 12 noon, longer pay for that kind of appointment, and that if these officers are to be paid, authority of law must be procured. And I understand the minister is getting the authority under this Bill.

Before asking for this
legislation the minister ought to furnish the committee with the memorandum from the Auditor General.

Surely, the hon. gentleman is going very far. The responsible minister has risen in his place and

stated his reason for proposing this Bill, and that reason is that he has been notified by the Auditor General that this kind of appointment cannot any longer be paid for. Now the hon. gentleman says that before the Bill passes the minister should bring the proof. I do not think he should say that to a minister of the Grown.

I do not think that is asking too much. The Department of Inland Revenue has been in operation since Confederation-for nearly fifty years. The minister tells us that temporary employees have been appointed from time to time during all that period and no objection has been raised. Now, I cannot think it possible that that has been done contrary to the law. I cannot imagine for a moment that that is the cause of asking for this legislation. It is no reflection upon the judgment of the minister to ask that the memorandum of the Auditor General should be produced. It would be very interesting to the House to know how it comes that this which has been going on for fifty years is now found to be objectionable under the law. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) must forgive me if I am a little suspicious as to the reason for this. We know that when this Government first came into office they wanted to get rid of the commissioners engaged for the construction of the National Transcontinental railway. They did not like to dismiss them, but they passed a law reducing the number of commissioners to one. I remember that in New Brunswick, not long ago, the Government there wanted to get rid of a very valued official. They did not like to dismiss him-to do so would have offended the public very much. But they passed a law fixing an age limit which was just such as to exclude this man, and so he was removed from office by legislation. Now the Minister of Inland Revenue, perhaps, wants to dismiss a lot of temporary employees.
Not at all.

He wants to declare that they are not legally appointed, and he wants power to make legal appointments. That is, he can quietly let these employees retire from office without incurring the odium of making dismissals. If called upon later to justify this act, he could say, and say truthfully, that Parliament had declared that these gentlemen engaged in temporary work were not legally appointed and therefore were not in the employ of
the Government at all. He could say: I did not dismiss them; they passed naturally out of the Government's employ, and I have appointed new officers under the authority Parliament has given me. The hon. gentleman will forgive me, if, in the light of what has taken place in the three years since this Government took office, we on this side, at least I-and I only speak for myself-am a little suspicious as to the reason for the passing of this Bill.
M. BLONDIN:	I shall be pleased to
give a copy of the memorandum to my hon. friend. He asks under what authority the department has been proceeding for years. The Auditor General did not refer particularly to the present; he referred to the condition under the late Government as well. We are simply making a provision similar to that which applies to the Customs Department.
The minister will produce that memorandum?
Yes.
What is the classification of the officials of the Inland Revenue Department?
There are four classes: special excisemen and first, second and third-class excisemen.
Are all the officers of the second division in the outside service?
Yes.

the minister stated a few moments ago jthat temporary employees should not receive higher salaries than the officials whom they replace. Are these temporary employees appointed simply to replace other officials,, or in addition to the regular permanent staff of the department?
These temporary officers are employed only when required. The intent of this proposed legislation is to provide for the appointment of temporary employees, who are paid only very small salaries.
Are they to be appointed only when certain permanent officials are ill or on leave of absence, or are they to be appointed in addition to the regular staff?
Most of these temporary officials are employed when the work increases to such an extent that their services are necessary.

Under a provision of the Inland Revenue Act, temporary employees may be appointed by Order in Council. I quote section 12:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, appoint officers and other persons to carry out this Act and all other Acts relative to the matters and things placed under the control and management of the department, and also all Orders in Council or regulations made there- ' under, and the Governor in Council may assign the names of office of such officers and persons, and grant them such salaries or pay for their labour and responsibility as he deems reasonable and necessary, and may appoint the times and manner in which the same shall be paid; but no such, officer or person shall receive a higher annual salary than is allowed in his case by the Civil Service Act.
It is clear, therefore, that the Governor in Council has at the present time power to appoint permanent or temporary officers all over the Dominion to positions in the outside service as well as in the inside service. My hon. friend is trying to-day, for some reason which he has not fully explained to. the committee, to take that power out of the hands of the Governor in Council and to place it in the hands of the minister. Is that in the public interest? Is there any reason for it? What is to hinder the minister from making his recommendations to council in respect of the appointment of temporary or permanent officers throughout the Dominion, as Las been the custom for the last fifty years?
The only answer I can give my hon. friend is that we are asking only for such power as is given to the ot) er departments.

Does the minister not agree with me that the Governor in Council, on his recommendation, may, under section 12 of the Act which I have jnst read, appoint temporary officers for work m any part of Canada?

I do not see why my hon. frrend. should wish to deprive my department of a privilege which it was deemed wise to extend to the other departments of Government. That is the only answer that I can give.

Perhaps the necessity for it has not been felt in my hon. friend's department.	*

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Sir George Foster, Bill No. 113, to amend the Gold and Silver Marking-Act, was read the second time and the House went into committee thereon, Air. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-offences made punishable on summary conviction, and minimum penalties added:

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The purpose of
this amendment is simply to provide better means for the enforcing of the Act. There is no change at all in any of the provisions of the Bill. In the first place the amendment is to provide that one who violates the Act shall be liable to summary conviction. Before, it was merely an indictable offence. This makes the procedure more simple and enables prosecutions to be made before the magistrate. Up to the present the supervisor or superintendent of the Act has had great difficulty in enforcing it on account of the delays that took place. The amendment also asks that the minimum fine be $25. The maximum is already fixed at $100. It also provides that the articles in regard to which a conviction is obtained under the Act shall be confiscated to the Crown. This conforms to the legislation in the Customs Act and the Criminal Code. Another amendment makes it possible for the inspector to seize articles
which he believes are in contravention of the Act, and to hold the same until the case is disposed of. Hitherto all he was able to do was to make an inspection and report, and then before the courts could take the matter up the articles would mysteriously disappear and the evidence was gone.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Could this summary
conviction be had before an ordinary justice of the peace?

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In our part of the country we are very far away from any inspector.
I have in mind a certain case where a more or less unprincipled jeweller came into the town and imposed upon the people very much. He carried on business quite a long time, selling watches and other things, and made a great deal of money. I remember being waited on by a deputation of the permanent jewellers, but the trouble seemed to be to get any inspector, and it occurred to me then whether ' the inspectors are conveniently situated gedgraphically. I should like to ask the minister about that.

maintopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
When the Act
came into force one inspector was appointed, and he does the work for the whole Dominion. He makes periodical trips through different parts of the country, and if there are any cases such as my hon. friend has mentioned he is informed about it. However, it is not necessary for him to be in any particular place in order to enable proceedings to be taken. This Act has been in force only a short time and has worked well, although the machinery for proper prosecution has been inefficient. In some cases offences against the Act have been thoroughly dealt with, but in more cases there was such delay and difficulty in getting evidence that the prosecutions did not turn out satisfactorily. There is probably more need of these amendments and of a better enforcement of the Act at present than heretofore, because the conditions of the country are such as rather to place a premium on the sale of cheap goods, and many people are being grossly imposed upon. They think they are getting fairly good jewellery, when really they are getting nothing but pinchbeck. The department proposes to see that the Act is enforced and, providing the expense is not too great, the proper machinery will he added as it becomes necessary.

speechtext:
The clause says " who being a dealer." Would that apply to a

What is the particular cause that has led up to the granting of this relief for destitute Indians? There are very few Indians in that part of Saskatchewan where they had a crop failure. There must be some other cause than the failure of crop. I would like some information on the point.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of Interior):
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This includes the Northwest, but it has largely to do with the outlying Indians. The information I have is that the outbreak of hostilities in Europe has affected the Indians to a considerable extent. The war has interfered with the fur trade, the European market for furs has disappeared for the time being, and the Indians' source of supplies has almost vanished, as they have no market for their furs and cannot get goods in trade for them, as the fur-traders will not accept the furs or make advances to the Indians in the form of supplies to enable them to go to their hunting grounds. The Indians are advised to hunt for food, and many are doing so, but nevertheless they have to be assisted. The department, through trading companies and the Northwest Mounted Police, have organized a system of relief for Indians requiring assistance, and as the vote for such requirements under normal circumstances is proving inadequate to meet the demand under the changed conditions, a supplementary grant becomes necessary.
What particular localities are likely to receive assistance under this grant?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is in the outlying and extreme northerly portions of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba.
There are no agents in these outlying districts. By what means is the relief to be distributed?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It is distributed largely through orders of the missionaries.
Do I understand that it is distributed entirely on the orders of the missionaries, or is there a division of authority ?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It will also be distributed through the Northwest Mounted Police where there are mounted police.

Either through the
mounted police or the missionaries?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Yes.
It does not rest with the trading companies?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.
Is there any destitution among the Indians of St. Peter's reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There has been nothing reported to the department. They are doing pretty well, I understand. They have had smallpox there.

I understand that some days ago an opportunity was taken, while discussing the affairs of the Indian Department, to place before the House certain statements in regard to a transaction in relation to the St. Peter's Indian reserve, which was intended to be a reflection upon the administration of the Indian Department, and a criticisni of the transaction by which the surrender of this reserve was secured.
I am sorry I was not present at the time, but I do not think it would be fair to the House or to the country to allow the opportunity to pass without placing before the House in as short a form as possible tne present position in regard to this reserve. There is a somewhat complicated series of accusations. One is that the Indians were not properly treated by the Government. In regard to that, I can only say that a treaty was made with the Indians for the surrender of the reserve. They were paid in accordance with the usual practice as to treaty payments, and over and above the price

that they received for the reserve, they received in exchange another reserve of greater area and better adapted to their requirements. Therefore the Indians were not mistreated in the transactions between them and the Government.
In regard to the attitude of the department and the circumstances of the surrender; the surrender was taken as other surrenders in Canada have been taken up to the present time. The vote of the majority of the band present decided in fa,vour of the surrender, and in accordance with that vote the surrender was made. After the surrender had been made, after the arrangements had been made for transferring the Indians to the new reserve, the Government of Manitoba stepped in and refused to register under the Land Titles Act of that province the transfers of land from the Indians to the parties who had bought from them. From that time to the present those transfers have not been registered, the responsibility being upon the Government of the province of Manitoba. The Government of the Dominion of Canada had bought the land from the Indians; it had paid the Indians for the land; the transaction was absolutely in accordance with the practice relating to such transactions in the past, and there was no reason or ground for the action of the Government of the province of Manitoba except a desire and intent to use not its right but its power as a means of blackmailing the purchasers of those lands. The Government of Manitoba saw fit to appoint a commission to inquire into the validity of the transaction on the part of the Dominion Government. That inquiry could have no possible effect except as an academic inquiry; but the commission made the inquiry, and the result of it was a finding that the transaction had been regular throughout, except that one part of the commission held the belief that the vote of the Indians for the surrender should have been a vote of an actual majority of the band and not a vote of the majority of those present.
Which commission was that?

A commission appointed
by the Government of the province of Manitoba. I do not know which commission; but there was a commission appointed that brought in that report.
As regards the validity of the surrender, if the vote of a majority of the band is necessary to a surrender, there has
been no surrender taken from the Indians in Canada which would be valid under that ruling; or if there is such a one, it is an exception. Therefore, if the suggestion that the surrender was illegal is correct, then the titles of land bought from Indian reserves throughout the Dominion of Canada are to-day invalid. Any one knows that if such a condition does exist, this Parliament will of necessity have to pass an Act validating those titles. Therefore there is no foundation in any way, shape or manner for the Government of Manitoba refusing the transfers, except as a means of enforcing blackmail upon the purchasers of those lands.
Without going into details, I may say that the position of this reserve was peculiar in many respects, and that it was necessary to make special arrangements in order to secure a surrender. Many unsuccessful attempts had been made to secure that surrender in times past. We made a further attempt and we were successful. It was believed that, although the terms granted to the Indians were extraordinary-and there is no doubt that they were extraordinary- it was in the interest both of the Indians and of the people who lived in that part of the province of Manitoba that the surrender should be secured and that the Indians should be removed to another reserve. Owing to the action of the Government of that province, owing to the suggestions that have been made to the Indians that under this, that, or the other set of circumstances they would be able to secure a larger payment for their land, all of them have not yet removed to this new reserve, and the reserve is to-day in very much the same position as it was when the surrender took place, the Indians being in a position that is entirely contrary to their welfare, and the surrounding locality including the town of Selkirk, is suffering very seriously and having its development retarded because of the failure of that surrender to be carried out.
On that point I have some information which 1 wish to place before the House, seeing that the matter has already been before us in so many ways.
I have here a copy of the Selkirk Weekly Record, a Conservative newspaper published in the town of Selkirk. This is the issue of January 22, and I will read from it a short article on the subject of this St. Peter's Indian Reserve:
St. Peter's and Selkirk.
The Record has repeatedly expressed its views on the above subject so vital to this district as

When the committee rose at one o'clock, I was reading an extract from the Selkirk Record of January 22, dealing with the subject of the St. Peter's Reserve. I wish to read another article on the same subject from the Record of January 29. It is headed:	" St. Peter's Reserve Question,"
and is as follows:

The public of this town and district are anxious to know what developments there are in the St. Peter's Reserve case. Several months ago it was officially stated that an action to annul the surrender had been commenced; that the writs were being served, and in twenty days the case would be brought to trial. From information that we have gathered as to this latest phase of the question we are forced to conclude that this announcement was deliberately made to deceive the public. There are over six hundred defendants in the action, all of whom must be served. Bach defendant has four weeks from the time he is served to reply. The trial can, therefore, not be reached until the last defendant has been served, and he has had time to reply. We leave it to our readers to figure out, from their knowledge of the speed with which our courts proceed when judgment may be expected.
To the authorities we would say: Stop playing with this question. Confirm the titles. The Indians are satisfied. While they realize that some of them made improvident sales, still the surrender contract was to them highly satisfactory alnd beneficial. The moral a,nd material advantages that followed the removal of the Indians from the old St. Peter's Reserve have far outweighed any wrong that the Indians may have sustained at the hands of unscrupulous land buyers. It is a well-known fact that Indians and half-breeds are prone to make improvident bargains, and quite frequently get the worst of the deal, and it may be taken for granted that many of the sales made by the St. Peter's Indians were no exception to the rule. Even if such were the case the cancellation of the surrender would instead of righting a wrong, result in a far greater wrong against many who are guilty of no wrong-doing.
The government would be rendering far greater assistance to the Indians if it would engage counsel, for those that have been cheated by individual buyers, to prosecute their case before the court of the province. It is now almost eight years since the surrender was taken. Does the Government now propose to give us another eight years of litigation? The public is-long suffering, but the limit has been reached.
I read from the Record of February 5:
It is safe to say that at least seventy-five per cent of the members of the St. Peter's Band of Indians wish the surrender to be confirmed. They realize that they made a good bargain with the Government and received very liberal treatment at its hands. A number of Indians have disposed of their lands at prices satisfactory to them but have not received payment in full because of the unsettled state of affairs now existing, and are suffering for the lack of these funds. The Government owes these a duty to ratify the surrender.
The present reserve is much more suitable for the purposes of the band than the St. Peter's Reserve, because the more isolated they are the easier it is for the chief and council and parents to control and guide the younger generation, and the evils which very often follow the intermingling of whites and Indians are cerrespondingly decreased.
Many fathers when voting for the surrender did so, no doubt, solely for the reason that they wished to get their children away from

the vicinity of the liquor traffic, and to avoid if possible the debauchery which so often follows in its trail, and because they hoped that the moral atmosphere of the new reserve would be more healthful than that of St. Peter's. This, we think, all will admit, is an important factor in the future welfare of the band. Are these fathers not entitled to as much consideration at the hands of the Government as some few members of the band, who imbibed too much whisky and then sold their lands for a song? The duty of the Government to its wards is as a strong in moral matters as in material, if not stronger.
If then the majority of the band wish to remain where they are and to have the surrender confirmed, why should the Government compel them, against their will and judgment, and to their decided disadvantage, to come back to St. Peters?
As has been pointed out in these columns cancellation of the surrender might benefit a few .individuals, but would harm a vastly greater number.
In the same issue, under the heading: " Public Meeting Needed/' I find the following:
The most important question now being discussed in Selkirk, next to the war, is the settlement of the St. Peter's land dispute. It is felt that the time has arrived for united action on the part of our citizens in demanding a speedy settlement of this long delayed matter, and it has been suggested that the Selkirk board of trade call a public meeting at an early date to discuss this question. The idea is a good one, and The Record hopes it will be carried out. The St. Peter's reserve question has too long been used as a political football to the detriment of our town, and it is high time our citizens made a vigorous protest. The Dominion Parliament is in session, and if a public meeting was held and a strong resolution passed, irrespective of politics, pointing out the great loss sustained by Selkirk, financially and otherwise, owing to the long delay in settlement, and a copy of such resolution forwarded to Premier Borden, some good might be accomplished. Since the surrender of the reserve, time and again we have been told that the matter in reference to the lands would be quickly settled, but the years have come and the years have gone and nothing has yet been done. Is it any wonder that the patience of our citizens is getting exhausted? The whole matter could be equitably adjusted in a short time if politics were not allowed to intervene. This question is not a political one, but a local one of vital interest to the welfare and progress of the town of Selkirk and district, and in this light it should be considered by the government. If any of the Indians have been defrauded there is a remedy, but justice should also be done to those who purchased the lands in good faith and have been deprived of their titles for years. Owing to the non-settlement of this question, some of the best land in the district has been lying idle for years, which, if a settlement had been made, would now have been occupied by good settlers and the town and district greatly benefited. By all means let a public meeting be called, and some definite action taken in an endeavour to have this hindrance to the prosperity and development of our town speedily removed.
Hon. gentlemen will observe that in the article that I have just read, the Record called for a public meeting and asked the Board of Trade to take action. The Record of February 12, under the heading: " Board of Trade, Annual Meeting," has the following:
The annual meeting of the Selkirk Board of Trade was held in the town hall on Thursday evening, February 4th. The report of the retiring council, presented by the President, F. A. Gemmel, dealt with the many matters that had come before the board during the past year, and concluded with a vigorous statement of the Board's portion with respect to the dilatory St. Peter's embrqglio, and an arraignment of the political tactics that had held up the settlement for eight years, ''eight years" in the language of the report, "of Western Canada's greatest development", eight years lost to Selkirk forever."
Before the annual meeting adjourned, a motion offered by mayor Ross and seconded by Bruce Campbell, was unanimously passed, congratulating The Selkirk Record upon the vi-goious and praiseworthy stand it has lately t .ken upon the St. Peter's question.
There is another article in this issue of the Record that I desire to read. I said that the Record is a Conservative paper. It is not and never was a Liberal paper; it is essentially and always has been a Conservative paper. In the article I am about to read it finds it desirable, in pursuance of its belief that nothing good can come from the Liberal side, to call in question the actions of the Liberal Government and myself, so that I think it is fair that the House should have the benefit of all that the paper has said on the subject, whether it reflects' on the Liberal Lrovernment and myself or not. The article is a retort to an article appearing in the Manitoba Free Press:
Playing Politics.
The Fress Press convicts the premier, and Mr. Bradbury of " playing politics " on the St. Peter's question.
That refers to the Premier of Manitoba.
The public know the facts. It is up to them now, but what about the Hon. Frank Oliver, who had most to do with this matter? Was he not warned by competent solicitors that there was a legal question demanding the attention of the Government as to whether the statutes required only a majority of the votes of the male members of a band over 21 years at the meeting, or whether it required a majority ol all the male members of the band over 21 years of age? His reply was that the St. Peter's Reserve was surrendered the same as all other reserves in Canada, and while this statement stands undisputed it is not a sufficient answer, and leaves a shadow not only on the titles of St. Peter's Reserve, but all other surrendered Indians in reserves in Canada. This was made very plain to him, and he was earnestly entreated to remove this possible technicality, and not hand out the title with a shadow or pos-

sible question mark on it But no, he and his party, must be sustained, and instead of giving: the relief asked for he proceeded to " play politics," and so the game goes on back, and forth while the interests of Selkirk and district are ground to dust under the feet of politicians. Now we are told with all seriousness that the case is in court. What is there to try? Nothing but the legal quibble just referred to that is common to all surrenders.
Newspapers and politicians may talk glibly with this surrender, but they are just " playing about fraud, and make sinister expressions about the dock doings in connection with this surrender, but they are just " playing politics," and they know it.
