(Mr. Bradbury), who has taken a very deep interest in the matter of the surrender of the reserve, has from time to time laid great stress upon the injustice that was done the Indians in this transaction. That injustice was in paying them for the land that they had, and giving them in the place of it a greater area of better land. My hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) shakes his head. He is inclined to deny the latter part of my statement. I propose to read to him the opinion of the Indian agent as to the benefit to the Indians of their removal to the new reserve. In the annual report of the Department of Indian Affairs for the year ended March 31, 1914, he says:
The movement of the people from St. Peter's continues, it has not been as rapid as I hoped it would be. Those who are still in residenec at St. Peter's have been advised that the time for receiving assistance from the department for moving- and building has about expired, and it has been pointed out to them that the advantage gained in this way is too valuable for them to'run any risk of losing it; there is now a pretty definite intention to move, one or two of the leaders have gone, and I hope to see many others arrange to do so during the coming season. Arrangements have been made to assist them in building, when they arrive at Peguis; a sufficient quantity of lumber and other building material has been placed there with Agent Carter, during the past winter, to meet any demands made for this purpose. It iy realized by them that they will be acting in their own best interest, if they move, as they find that those who have moved are doing well at Peguis.
I think I may rest the case there for the present. We now have the evidence as to the benefit the white people derive from the taking of this surrender, and it is given by those who are in a measure entitled to speak for the white people. We also have the evidence of the officers of the department as to the benefit to the Indians of their taking advantage of the arrangement that was made. I think under those circumstances my hon. friend from Selkirk will have to consider that he is in a minority on this question.

The hon. member for Edmonton, the ex-Minister of the Interior in the late Government (Mr. Oliver), the man responsible for this transaction, speaking before the House rose at one o'clock, made some statements in my absence which I deem it wise to refer to. But before doing so I wish to refer to one or two things that [DOT] he said just before he resumed his seat.
Speaking of the advantage that has accrued to the St. Peter's Indians from the surrender, the hi n. gentleman would seek

to leave the impression on the people that the surrender was a good thing for the Indians. Let us examine for a moment that feature of the matter. St. Peter's Indian Reserve was adjacent to the town of Selkirk; in fact, it formed a part of that town. It comprised 48,000 acres within 26 miles of Winnipeg. That land is worth to-day $2,500,000 if it is worth a dollar. On the evidence of some men that the hon. gentleman has quoted as bet ig present at that meeting, and asking that these titles should be validated, this land was worth at the time of the surrender on an average of $25 an acre for the 48,000 acre;. The hon. gentleman seeks to leave the impression that it was a good bargain for the Indians that this change had taken place. The Government and those who desired the surrender of this 48,000 acres of the most valuable land in Manitoba, selected a site 90 miles farther north, along the west shore of lake Winnipeg, and gave the Indians 70,000 acres of land there in lieu of the 48,000 acres they had taken from them. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that this land compared in value with the 48,000 acres taken from the Indians? Every man who knows anything about wild land in that part of Manitoba knows that from $3 to $4 an acre would be a good value to place upon this 70,000 acres of land. He acquired land from the Indians that was worth at the time it was taken $25 to $50 an acre. He took an estate from the St. Peter's Indians which is worth at least to-day $2,500,000. I ask if that is considered fair treatment of the Indians of this country.
The hon. gentleman says that I have taken a great interest in the Indians. I have. And why? It is not because I have any personal interest in them, not because there was any political kudos to be gained from it; the Indian has no vote, he has no influence, he has no money. I was in the town when this outrageous transaction took place and I would have been lass than a man, I would have been unworthy of the position which' I occupy in this House if I had not attempted to rectify that shameful transaction and expose it to this country. I thought that when I appealed to the minister of the Interior of that time, the present hon. member for Edmonton, and, when he became seized of the facts, that I had laid before this House, he would take action and do some-.-thing to rectify the great wrong which had been perpetrated on the St. Peter's Indians. But the hon. gentleman satis-

fled himself with taking up three hours of the time of the House in an attempt to 'dispute the charges which I had made and when he sat down he left every charge unanswered and the charge made by me against the Indian Department just as strong as it was before he rose to his feet. During every session from 1907 to 1911, I appealed to the hon. gentleman across the floor of this House to do something to relieve the situation and to see that a modicum of justice was done to the poor unfortunate Indians, but I appealed in vain. The hon. gentleman made no attempt to settle the question. The late Government should have settled that question immediately, but when their attention was called to the matter in this House the present hon. member for Edmonton, the man who is responsible for this transaction, sat tight in his place and allowed the matter to drift year after year without making any attempt to settle it although he was appealed to time and time again across the floor, of this House and appealed to by residents oT the town of Selkirk in just as strong articles as he has read from the Record to-day. Yet he made no attempt to settle the matter. He said: What we have done, we have done, the surrender was legal and it must stand. That is the position he took. The statements I made when I opposed the trms-action I made after the most thorough investigation, I made with a full knowledge of my responsibility as a member of this House, and six or seven years having elapsed since that time, I have not one word to retract of what I said on that occasion.
Would the hon. gentleman briefly state what were the charges that he made?
I will state some of them briefly. It would take too long to recite all of them.
I do not want the hon. gentleman to take too long.

The charges were that the Indians had been fraudulently deprived of their very valuable estate, that the meeting called for the surrender had been manipulated by the Indian agent and by the officers of the Indian Department, that the meeting where this surrender was declared to be carried was advertised for but one day, that twenty-four hours' notice was all the time that was given to the band of Indians to gather and decide as to the surrender.
119J
What year was that?

That was in 1907.
This reserve is about ten miles square. Many of the young Indians, at that season of the year, were at lake Winnipeg fishing. There must have been thirty or forty of the young members of the band who never heard of this meeting. I have under my hand now the testimony of men living within a mile of the place where this surrender was voted on, and these men swear that they never knew that the meeting was being held. Another charge was that the Indian Act had been violated, that clause 49 of the Act provided that a majority of the male members of the band of 21 years of age at the meeting must vote in favour of the surrender or the surrender would not be valid. That is a point in regard to which my hon. friend from Edmonton and I differ. I remember that when we were discussing this point, he was arguing in favour of the clause, and I asked him if a meeting was called where there were two hundred and some odd qualified voters, and if only twenty voters attended that meeting, could those twenty Indians legally alienate the interest of all the rest of the Indians? My answer to that question is that they could do it legally hut perhaps not morally. I want to say to the hon. gentleman that in the opinion of two of the most reputable judges we have in Manitoba the position that the hon. gentleman had taken is utterly unjustifiable. A report was made by a Royal Commission appointed by the: Manitoba Government and composed of three county court judges-Judges Prudhomme, Myers and Locke. Every hon. gentleman who comes from the West knows' the reputation of these men. After a thorough examination of the whole case, two reports were brought in, a majority report and a minority report, but Judge Lc-ke, speaking for himself and Judge Prudhomme, says:
The surrender was not only voidable but void, and could not be ratified and should not be ratified.
That is the decision of those men at that time. Still the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who was responsible for the transaction, for three long years while he was minister of the department that perpetrated this transaction, made no attempt to rectify it. The consequence is that it has been handed down as a heritage to the present Government. I have not argued out of the House and I am not going to argue. in the House that the matter has been expe.
Who is Mr. Pedley?

He was the Deputy
Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs.
Is he in office now?

No, he has been re- moved, or he resigned, I understand. I am not going to say that Mr. Pedley was to blame, for that would be taking an unfair advantage of an official of the department. The minister of that time must take the blame and so must the Government of which he was a member. I do not think, for a moment, that the deputy minister went out and negotiated and secured that surrender without the full consent of his minister. 'Consequently, what was done in securing the surrender, was done, I take it, with the full knowledge of that minister. But I must say that as hon. members who recollect the defence that that gentleman put up for that transaction will know, he displayed such utter ignorance of what had taken place that I should hesitate, to believe, even now, that he really did know what was done in this matter, though, as head of the department, he is responsible.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) made the statement that if this surrender was illegal, every other surrender taken up to the present moment, was equally illegal. He is not well informed. The present Government composed of men who, when in Opposition condemned what the late Government did in this connection, took precautions to settle this matter, and not one surrender
has been taken since this Government came into power in which the Indian Act has not been lived up to scrupulously. That there may be no misunderstanding let me quote clause 5 which takes the place of clause 49 of the Indian Act:
A surrender must be assented to by a majority of the Indians whose names appear on the voters' list, who must he present at the meeting or council summoned for the purpose as hereinafter provided.
This makes plain what interpretation should have been placed on section 49. When the hon. gentleman made the statement that if the St. Peter's Indian surrender was illegal every other surrender in Canada was illegal, he is quite in error. Other surrenders taken before this matter was exposed in the House may have been as illegal as this, but I do not believe that there is anything in the records of Canada to show such a brazen attempt made to defraud the Indians as in the case of the St. Peter's Indian Reserve.
As to the matter published in the Selkirk Record and the Winnipeg Free Press, let me say this to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver):	He is proprietor of a newspaper and knows a good deal about editing a newspaper, and a good deal 4 p.m. about what reliance can be placed, sometimes, on the actions of a newspaper. There has been, during the last six weeks, a campaign to stampede the present Government into a settlement of this question, not only against the interest of the Indians, but against the interest of the people of Canada and against the interest of the town of Selkirk. For I say now from my place in Parliament, and with all due deference to my friends, some cf whom are connected with these resolutions, and with all due deference to the Record, that, so far as the town of Selkirk is concerned, to my mind the greatest crime that could be committed against the town v.culd be to validate the titles of the St. Peter's Indian Reserve and hand this property over to a bunch of grafters, men who will hold the land at exorbitant prices for years to come and prevent the very result that the people want, viz., the settling up of that district. The late Government professed that they were working in the interests of the people, that they held the land in trust for the people and believed in the policy of " the land for the settlers and not lor tue speculators." Had they lived up to this policy they could have purchased from the Indians at a reasonable figure, and that

would have satisfied the Indians, forty-eight thousand acres of the best land in Manitoba. Then we should have had every acre of it settled by bona fide settlers to-day, but instead of that the Government of that day chose to play into the hands of a few speculators and only certain men could purchase these lands. A Conservative in the town of Selkirk at that time was told by the Indian agent that he need not attempt to buy the lands, that the department could give him no protection, and that he would be buying at his own risk. But Mr. Heap, a leading Liberal, Mr. Funk, a brother of Senator Funk of the United States, a very wealthy man, Mr. Frank of Winnipeg, another strong Liberal, and Mr Tracy of Se'kn-k, another strong Liberal- these were the men who bought from the Indians the lands all the way from one d far to five dollars and six dollars an acre. God knows how the Indian was paid, for the Indian himself does not know. When he went in to make a payment, he got, perhaps, a ten-dollar bill, and was asked to sign a receipt for it, and that receipt was a deed for the man's property, and nobody knows what he got afterwards. There is a letter on file from the Indian agent himself, who was in this transaction, who told his minister that after the first payment was made it depended entirely upon the honour of the purchaser what the Indian got. That is a sample of what was done and of what the hon. member for Edmonton would urge the Government to legalize. Why, if the Government of Canada were to legalize an action of this kind which has been exposed and proven, all I say is that there is very little justice for the poor unfortunate Indian.
I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in dealing with this attempt made by my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) to revive this case in the House. His advice to the Government is, practically, to validate these titles. Let us see how that would work out. Does he mot know-I am sure he does-that the Registrar General of Manitoba has refused to issue a Torrens title on these patents issued by the Government and that before a Torrens title can issue some action must be taken by Parliament? Now, if that is true is that not evidence that the transaction was illegal in the first place, and if it was illegal why shouiu it be legalized. I want to say, in passing, that I regret as much, and more, than the hon. gentleman rrom Edmonton, that this case was not settled years ago. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) ought to

have settled this question before he went out of office-, but he let the matter rest for three years without taking action. It may be said that that does not justify the delay on the part of the present Government. I am not going to argue that it does. This matter ought to have been settled, and those who had been in authority will bear me out when I say that no one has been more persistent than I have been in attempting to secure a settlement of this case year after year. I did not suggest the settlement that the hon. member for Edmonton wishes; I urged that the matter be taken to court and, if the surrender be proved legal, that the registrar general of Manitoba should recognize the patents and settle the matter for all time to come. The case is now, I understand, ready for trial in the Exchequer Court. It is worthy of remark that the very men who have been clamouring for a settlement of this case for the last four years have been making every effort possible to block the proceedings which have been taken to make it possible to secure an early settlement. What have these men to feaT? If their conduct has been free from blame, why should they hesitate to allow this matter to go before the Exchequer Court for the opinion of the judge as to its legality? It is like the Irishman who went to an eminent lawyer when he was in trouble, and asked for his assistance. The eminent lawyer assured him that he would secure justice for him. "Well," said Pat, "it is not justice I want; I want to get out of this difficulty." And I think that some of the men who have obtained these lands do not want justice; they want to get the titles to the lands. This .question ought to be settled, and the men who have secured these lancts-some of which, I have no hesitation in saying, were literally stolen from the Indians-should not be allowed to retain them without recompensating the Indians in some way. Six of these men secured 35,000 acres of lands at less than $5 an acre: land which is the most valuable in the province of Manitoba, and which without any doubt, is worth to-day from $50 to $60 an acre. It is not too much to ask these men, even at this late date, to do justice to the Indians? My hon. friend stated that about half of this land was sold by public auction. That, of course, is in line with many other statements made by the hon. gentleman; it is not quite in accordance with the facts. Only about 15,000 acres out of 48,000 were sold by public auction. And how were they sold? The auction sale was manipulated just as skillfully as the

land itself was manipulated. The Department of Indian Affairs advertised the sale in six different issues of the Toronto Globe and the Winnipeg Free Press. The sales took place, I think, on December 16. There was a foot of snow on the ground; the advertisement had been withdrawn eighteen days before the sale took place, so that the public did not know anything about the sale when it did take place. The men who attended the sale were largely the same men who negotiated with the Indians for thieir little holdings; these are the men who got the land. No attempt was made by the Indian Department to secure a fair price for these lands.
How many people were at the sale?

I did not attend the
. sale, but I am told that in the morning there were present from five to ten men who represented these big holdings and fifteen or twenty Ruthenians who were anxious to obtain cheap land. These Ruthenians, by their bidding, made the other men bid up, and I understand that some of the land which was sold in the morning realized a price as high as $7 or $8 an acre. At lunch time an arrangement was made whereby a man was paid to take these foreigners into a barroom and keep them there until after the sale was finished. This is history; it is common knowledge in the town of Selkirk.
What did the department have to do with that?

Nothing at all; but
the department should not have allowed the sale to take place under the conditions that it did. Imagine the trustee of an estate selling a valuable piece of land in the middle of winter.

The hon. gentleman referred a few minutes ago to a report of the commission of judges appointed by the local government of the province of Manitoba. As I understand the matter, the two judges based their decision not upon the existence of fraud in connection with the sale of these lands, but upon the question of the interpretation of section 49 of the Indian Act.

To some extent that
is so, but not altogether. When the case was referred to these judges, the public understood that they were going to investigate not only the question of legality, but the question of alleged fraud as well. Judge Locke and Judge Prudhomme, in making their report, said this:
One phase at a time. However, we thought it would be desirable to report on the validity of the surrender first and leave it to the Government to decide as to whether or not it is necessary for the commissioners in view of this finding proceed with the other branch of the duties entrusted to them.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
They gave the Indians distinctly to understand that further investigation would be made into the fraudulent transactions between the purchasers and the Indians. This has never taken place. That is where I think the present Government have been entirely too lenient; they should have pushed the matter home more fully than they did.
I realize just as the men in Selkirk and all over the country' realize, that this case ought to be settled and I am just as anxious as a.ny man could be that it should be settled. I believe that the proper way is to settle this thing in court. There can be no question that if the surrender is legal the men who have got the land should be willing to allow the matter to go to the Exchequer court where it could be settled in a week. I made an offer five years ago to these men. I had authority to do it from the Registrar General of Manitoba. I was trying to gat a settlement then and urged upon him to point out some way of settling it. He said: Get these men to take an action in court to force me to issue a Torrans title to any one of these properties; and if they make good, if they can get a judgment in their favour, I shall issue the title. That was a fair proposition, and if the men who had the land were satisfied that they were right and had nothing to hide or fear, would it not have been easy for them to take the case to court and ask the decision of the Manitoba court, where they had all their friends, Chief Justice Howell, who was a party to securing the surrender, being Chief Justice of Manitoba at the time. They did not dare take it to the courts because they knew that they had not a leg to stand on; and they have been working ever since trying to secure from the Government some legislation that will validate those titles.
During my last election, in 1911, these men spent thousands of dollars frying to defeat me in my county on account c* what I had done in this transaction. No man in this House or out of it has ever insinuated or dared to insinuate that 1 had any personal interest in this matter. My action was dictated entirely in the interest of justice to the Indian who could not defend himself and the best interests

of my own town of Selkirk to make it impossible for 48,000 acres adjacent to the town, some of it within the limits of the town, to be tied up in the hands of speculators. I hold yet that I was justified in everything I did in trying to prevent these speculators from getting control of these lands.
The case is now in the hands, as I understand, of the Exchequer Court, and I hope it will come to trial very soon and that it will not stop there. I hope action will be taken to punish the men who have fraudulently dispossessed the Indians of their lands. There are men who have secured these lands as I have said before, who have literally stolen them from the Indians. These men ought to be prosecuted and punished, and it is up to the Indian Department to see that this is done.

On several occasions when this matter has been discussed in the House I have taken some part in the discussion, and that is my reason for rising to-day. I have no concern about the quarrel the hon. member for Selkirk has with some of his constituents in regard to this question, the only interest I have in the matter is the question of whether or not the administration of the Indian Department under the late Government was properly carried out in connection with the surrender'of the St. Peter's Indian Reserve. There is no question that for several years prior to the surrender in 1907 the people of Sel.urk and the surrounding country were continually asking that this surrender be obtained.

That statement was made, I think, by the then Minister of the Interor, now the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). There is not a line of evidence to justify that statement. The people of Selkirk never asked that the surrender should be made, nobody ever asked for it except the late member for Selkirk, Mr. Jackson. That was brought out in evidence.

My hon. friend may be better informed in that regard than I am, but I always understood that in and around Selkirk, as in the case of the surrender of other reserves in Canada, there was a movement on the part of settlers for the surrender of the reserve. I understood when the matter was discussed previously in the House, four or five years ago, that that was the case, and it was on that basis that I made my statements.' The surrender was

arranged for in 1907 and, in so far as I have been informed, no objection was taken by any residents of that district to the surrender being made provided it was made properly. I think my hon. friend himself was in favour of the surrender.

So far as the town of Selkirk is concerned and myself personally, I agree with what was said by the hon. member for Edmonton, and I think it a good thing that the Indians have been moved; it is a good thing for themselves. But that does not justify robbing them.

The charges that were
made repeatedly by the hon. member for Selkirk and other members on that side of the House some years ago, and the charges repeated by him to-day, are that, first, there was fraud in connection with the surrender of the reserve, either on the-part of the department or on the part of men who subsequently bought these lands from the Indians, or on the part of both. A general charge was made that the Indians were fraudulently deprived of a very valuable asset. That is the main charge I have ever heard made, but, I have never seen an iota of evidence to support it. It is easy to talk about fraud, but when you come down to the basis of things and get to facts it is difficult to prove the existence of what is really meant by fraud, and I would point out that apart from departmental fraud altogether if my hon. friend refers to fraud on the part of individuals in the province of Manitoba in getting lands from the Indians or from the department in connection with this reserve, they have their remedy. Why does not the Attorney General of Manitoba prosecute these men? Then we will have the question disposed of once and for all. That would not, it is true, dispose of a charge of fraud on the part of the department. As to the charge of fraud on the part of the department or on the part of Mr. Pedley, it all comes down to this, that Mr. Pedley had $5,000 in a little black valise, and said to the Indians:	If this surrender goes through
to-day I can make a part payment on the purchase price. That is all he meant, he did not pretend to buy the Indians. What benefit would he or any other officer get by bribing the Indians to hand over their land, to give the surrender? That is the whole question.

I know the hon. gentleman wants to be fair. The facts are

these. The hon. member knows the Indian pretty well, probably as well as I do.
I do not admit that.

And he knows the effect of making a statement such as Mr. Pedley did make to the effect: I have $5,000 here, and if this surrender goes through this will be divided among you, and if it does not go through, you will not get anything. I do not for a minute dispute that the money was supposed to come out of the sale of the Indian lands.
I believe that myself, but the poor Indian did not understand it that way. He understood he was getting part of that $5,000.

Everybody who
pays any attention to Indian Estimates knows that there is a vote every year for the purpose of obtaining the surrender of Indian reserves. Only the other night there was one for $25,000. I understand that it has always been customary to pay the Indians a small sum of money when the surrender is arranged for. I do not know what words Mr. Pedley used. My hon.' friend knows, and I have no doubt he repeated the words correctly this afternoon. But considering the position Mr. Pedley occupied in the Indian Department, and that neither he nor any other Government official profited by this surrender, how could any reasonable man put the interpretation on these words that the hon. member for Selkirk has; namely, that Pedley wanted to bribe these Indians and led them to believe they would get this money, in addition to whatever price they got for their land. I know a little about Indians; I have seen some of them, although I am not so familial with them as my hon. friend from Selkirk, who is particularly familiar with the St. Peter's Reserve. But the Indian as a rule is a pretty shrewd man, and I have no doubt the Indians knew perfectly well that that $5,000 was a payment on account of the purchase price for the lands being surrendered, and that it was not in addition at all. The hon. member for Selkirk knows that perfectly well. That is the sum and substance of the charge of fraud, in so far as the deartment is concerned. With the exception o this $5,000, I have never heard of any ot: [DOT][DOT] charge being brought against the depart:, mt. I venture to say that not a court in the 'and would hold the officials of the department guilty of fraud on the evidence that has been produced by the hon. member for Selkirk from time to time. What is the
other charge he makes? He says the meeting was only advertised for a very short time.
Twenty-four hours.

I cannot lay my finger
upon it, but I understand the provision is that the meeting shall be called in accordance with the regulations of the band. What were the regulations of this band? I do not know, my hon. friend has not told us. In looking over this report I find that the judges expressed the opinion that sufficient notice of the meeting was not given, but they distinctly say that, so far as the evidence was concerned, they could not say that it was not called in accordance with the regulations of the band. Further, to substantiate the belief that the Indians were notified, there Is the fact that, at the meeting, out of 223 men who were entitled to vote 205 were present.
The hon. gentleman has not got the vote right. There were 289 qualified votes in St. Peter's band at the time, and 205 were present.

Two hundred and twentythree are the figures I have but I may be mistaken. At any rate 205 out of 289 is a fairly good representation. In so far as any proceedings in court are concerned, I venture the opinion that the whole matters simmers down, not to a question of fraud at all, but to the question of the interpretation of section 49 of the Indian Act; and in the report that was presented to the Manitoba Government by the commission of judges appointed by that province, one of the three judges puts an altogether different interpretation on that clause from the other two. Two of tire judges say that a majority of the whole Band must vote at the meeting. The other one says that the proper interpretation is that the vote must , be supported by a majority of those present at the meeting. Let me read the clause to the House:
Except as in this Parliament otherwise provided, no release or surrender of a reserve, oi a portion of reserve, held for the use of the Indians of any band, or of any individual Indian, shall be valid or binding-, unless the release or surrender shall be assented to by a majority of the male members of the band of the full age of twenty-one years, at a meeting or council thereof summoned for that purpose.
As I said, one of the judges appointed by the province of Alanitoba saw fit to interpret the section to this effectr that a majority of those present was all that was required. The other two say that that is not correct. So there we have at least a

difference of opinion among judges who are eminently qualified to express an opinion upon the interpretation of that clause. When you consider that every surrender of a reserve has, up to the time of the surrender of the St. Peter's Reserve, always been carried out on that basis, I think we are justified in coming to the conclusion that a proper interpretation was. placed ixpon that clause, especially in view of' the fact that three judges of the land disagree on the matter.
If that is right, would it not have been a very easy matter for the Indian Departmnt to submit the case to the courts for decision? But they would not do that.

I am not here to
criticise the old Administration, but I would say this to my hon. friend: he has spent, and to my mind wasted>
a tremendous amount of the time of this House and of his own time during three or iour years. If the interpretation placed upon that Act by the ex-Minister of the Interior was not correct, why did not my hon. friend's friends rectify it as soon as they came into power?
Mr. BRADBURY. They should have done so.

The matter appears to
me'to be this way. There are a great many innocent purchasers of this land. My hon. friend does not mean to say that all the men who purchased this land from the Indians were guilty of fraud. No; a large proportion of them are innocent purchasers. That being the case, it is very difficult for ine to understand how the Provincial Government can step in to the Land Titles Office and say:	You shall not issue patents to
the hundreds of men who have purchased the land quite innocently. In order to make political capital out of this matter against the late Government, and in an endeavour to show that the late Governmeent did not deal fairly with the Indians and the natural resources of this country, my hon. friend resorted to the Roblin Government for the purpose of creating a political furore about this particular surrender. And now the chickens are coming home to roost.

As I understood it
from the Registrar General, the Manitoba Government had absolutely nothing to do with it. It was the Registrar General himself on his own responsibility, because he is responsible to the Government for every

title he issues, and my hon. friend as a lawyer knows that.

I do not know anything
of the kind.
It is absolutely right.
The Government of Manitoba is responsible.

The Government of
Manitoba is responsible to the people, and the Registrar General to the Government. The consequence was that when the Rigis-trar General refused to issue those titles, the Government in its own defence appointed this commission to demonstrate whether 'the Registrar General was justified in what he was doing. That explains the situation if I understand it correctly, and I think I do. That is the only attempt the Manitoba -Government made to get this matter settled, and if the commission had found out that the patents had been issued properly and the surrender taken legally, there would have been no question about it.
Air. A1ARTIN:	The Manitoba Government and the hon. member for Selkirk, for the purpose of making political capital out of this question and throwing discredit on the late Government, got the Registrar General to refuse to issue the patents.

No man can dictate
to Mr. McAra, the Registrar General of Manitoba.

The Government of the
province of Manitoba appointed a commission of three judges for the purpose of see-* ing what kind of a surrender this was, and to investigate the charges of fraud. The judges all expressed the opinion that there was no fraud at all on the part of the Indian Department. You can read the report from one end to the other and you will not find a word as to fraud on the part of the Indian Department. So it is a question of the interpretation of section 49 of the Indian Act, and that is all there is to it, and that seems to me a very small question to have taken up so much of the time of the House in the last six or seven years. There was a time, when, listening to the remarks of my hon. friend at such extended length, I began to think that there might be something wrong. Having taken occasion to look into the matter I came to the conclusion then, as I believe to..-day that section 49 is absolutely the only thing that is at issue in connection with this whole matter. I venture the opinion that

in the ease that is before t'he Exchequer Court to-day, unless some fraud can he established against some one or more of these purchasers, every one of them will get his patent.
Now let us consider for a moment what took place in connection with the sale. My hon. friend- says that this land is worth $2,500,000. He knows that when he says that he talks rubbish. It means $50 or $60 per acre for ordinary farm land. Does my hon. friend say that that land is as valuable as land on Portage Plains or in the Neepawa district?
Yes, I mean to say that no land in Manitoba is as valuable as the St. Peter's Reserve land.

My hon. friend calls into question the genuineness of the auction sale and casts aspersions upon the conduct of those who had to do with it. It is a difficult matter to carry out an understanding between an auctioneer and 200 or 300 purchasers at an auction sale. My hon. friend says that a great many foreigners went to this sale expecting to be able to get some farm land.- How did they expect to get cheap farm land at St. Peter's Indian Reserve when, according to the hon. gentleman, that land was worth $50 or $60 an acre? In any event, in so far as the Indians were 'concerned, they got 25,000 acres of land. I do not know how many acres were sold; I understand that 25,000 acres were sold, but my hon. friend says that there were only 15,000 acres sold. If there were only 15,000 acres sold then there are 10,000 acres left to the credit of the Indians. At all events they got the benefit of the sale of 15,000 acres of land and the proceeds of that sale go to their credit in the Indian Trust Fund. In addition to that the Indians' got 20,000 acres in severalty. At the- auction sale 15,000 acres of farm land were sold. There were over a hundred people at that sale, there was open bidding, 15,000 acres of land were purchased and the average price paid was only $5.76 per acre.

I would like to correct my hon. friend when he makes the statement that there were over a hundred people at the sale because he is stating something that is absolutely contrary to the fact. There never were more than twenty people at the sale and more than half of them were foreigners.

The information I have is altogether contrary to that. I was not
present, of course, and my hon. friend was not present, and he does not know anything more about it than I do.
It took place in my town.

My information is that the sale was largely attended and my hon. friend's information is that there was a very small attendance. However, we will not delay over that question. As a matter of fact school lands sold in Manitoba in that very same year did not produce any more per acre.
And the school lands were offered on more favourable terms.

Yes, under a ten-year term. We know that in the West, where a large quantity of land is put on the market at once, it is not an uncommon thing for ordinary farm land to go fairly cheap at an auction sale. Sometimes cases occur where a piece of land close to a town is offered for sale, a lot of people living in the town want to buy it and the price runs up far beyond the value of farm land. But the fact is that at this auction sale 15,000 acres of land, notwithstanding the fact that every person who dealt in real estate in Winnipeg knew that the sale was going to be held, sold for $5.76 per acre. The people of the town of Selkirk knew that this sale was being held. My hon. friend knew it; why did he not go to the sale with some of his friends and see that the Indians got their just due? In addition to that, the portion of the 20,000 acres that the Indians got in severalty realized from $3 to $20 per acre: It does not appear to me that in connection with this sale the Indians were defrauded. In so far as the question of the Indians being defrauded by purchasers is concerned, if what my hon. friend says is true, it is the duty of the Attorney General's Department of the province of Manitoba to immediately prosecute those men who have defrauded these Indians out of their lands.
Do you not think it is the duty of the Indian Department as the guardian of the Indians?

Well, then my hon. friend has influence with the Indian Department; he might exert it. He has taken three and a half years to get nothing done. The late Government did not do anything on his representations because they did not believe that there was anything whatever in the charges that the hon. gentleman made. When the judgment of the Exchequer Court

is given, if these cases ever come to trial, I venture to give my opinion that he will find that there is nothing in them. The Indian will be exactly where he was seven or eight years ago and the town of Selkirk, and the purchasers who have been held up for their patents, will be exactly in the same position as they were in seven or eight years ago. In one of the articles quoted by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) the statement was made that the town of Selkirk has lost seven or eight years of its development by reason of the agitation which has been carried on.
My hon. friend says that the Indians were further defrauded in that they were not given a chance to get their patents direct but that somebody else got them. My information is that there were 400 patents issued for each one of which the Indian Department obtained a receipt and that these receipts are in the Department of Indian Affairs to-day. The department refused to recognize the assignment of an Indian's rights to another and they insisted on forwarding the patent directly to the Indian and getting his receipt. For that purpose the patents were sent to the Indian agent at Selkirk, he got the receipts immediately and the receipts are on file here. What fraud is there in that? In connectipn with the surrender of the St. Peter's Indian Reserve, the only question that has ever come before the committee at any time is the question as to whether or not the word "majority" in section 49 of the Indian Act means a majority of the men present at the meeting or a majority of the men who are entitled to vote in the trjbe.
Has the minister had any recent correspondence with the authorities in Sydney relative to the proposal to remove the Indians from the reserve near that city?

speechtext:

British Columbia-to provide a further amount for the relief of destitute Indians, $10,000.
What is the present condition of the Indians of the Kitsilano reserve, where are they located and what reports has the minister as to their present financial condition?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: ' There is no change in the situation as compared with what it was when we were discussing this question a year ago. The Indians were removed from the reserve and they went to other reserves, I understand. I have not heard that there has been any bad effect from the payment to the Indians to secure the surrender any more than there was in the case of the Indians in the neighbourhood of Victoria on the Songhees reserve. The case at the present time is before the Royal Commission. They have not adjudicated yet upon the case 'and that is the reason why I have nothing further to report than I brought to the attention of the House last session.

The reason I ask in regard to the condition of these Indians is because of the difference in their situation from that of the Songhees Indians. The Songhees Indians were paid fox one reserve and given another. The Kitsilano Indians were paid by the British Columbia Government, and they were not given another reserve. I was anxious to know exactly what had become of them, where they were located now and what their financial circumstances were. The minister will bear in mind that there is a very radical difference between the two conditions. The Songhees have a definite reserve to which they have clear title and which they are now in occupation of, whereas the Kitsilano Indians, so far as I know, have no reserve.

I think I can explain the matter if the minister will permit me. The hon. member is mistaken in the statement that the Kitsilano Indians have no reserve to go to. There are about half a dozen small reserves around Vancouver to which the Squamish band belongs, and I think that is the general name of the band. Only a very few of the Indians who claimed a right in the Kitsilano reserve, actually live on the reserve, and the rest are nomads so far as that reserve is concerned. Sometimes they go up the north sbc"e of Burrard inlet to the Squamish mission, sometimes to the Kapilano reserve or the Seymour reserve, iso that they are not homeless in. any sense. They have the other .sections of the district to which they go and where they are now living, and they are, as far as I know, living in very good circumstances. I do not know of any evil effects having come to the Indians from the transaction.
[Mr. W. M. Martin. 1

The hon. member's explanation is hardly adequate. If all the small reserves belong to the one band, the whole of the band had a right to share in any distribution of money in regard to one part of it.
That would not follow.

It does follow then that
those of the Ritsilano band who received the money on account of that reserve have no equal rights with the Indians occupying the other parcels of land said to be under the control of the Squamish band. My hon. friend cannot have it both yays. Either the band as a whole should have been. paid for that reserve, or those of the band who were paid have not equal rights with the other members of tne oand in the other reserves, and as a matter of fact they are either trespassers on the other smaller reserves or they are there on suffrance by the members of those bands. It is quite likely that Indians who have received large payments such as they did are very welcome amongst their fellow's, and very likely their circumstances are entirely satisfactory; but their condition is not parallel lo that of the Indians of the Songhees Reserve. Has there been any assumpu-on of occupation or ownership on the part of the Government of British Columbia in the Kitsilano Reserve?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No.

Does the Department of
the Interior assert and exercise supervision and control in the matter of necessary protection of property and so on upon that reserve at the present time-	[DOT]

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Tne position of the Department of the Interior is exactly as it was prior to the surrender of that reserve - to the Provincial Governm nt. We have not recognized that surrender in any way, shape, or form. Our position is exactly the same as tnougn the surrender had not taken place.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: As j say, there has been no change. No instructions have been given other than those which the agent received and was exercising prior to the surrender. As the hon. gentleman has stated, what few houses there were have been burned. The Indians have left the reserve. There is practically no jurisdiction to exercise; that is, there are no Indians to supervise; there is no property to protect, and the duty of the agent there would not be of a very onerous character.

The question that I
wanted to ask and that I think I may consider has been answered by the minister is whether the Indian Department of the Federal Government, or the Government of British Columbia exercises proprietary rights in the reserve. I would be bound to conclude that it is the Government of British Columbia which exercises those proprietary rights at the present time, and not the Department of Indian Affairs.

On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty (Minister of Justice), Bill No. 110, to amend the Dominion Elections Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1, section 61-Dominion Elections Act amended:	-

Perhaps the minister
would explain the purpose of the Bill and what the changes are?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is the Bill reported by the committee that was appointed to inquire into the Dominion Elections Act and the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, and to suggest amendments to them. The Bill is the result of the considerations of the committee, and has been unanimously submitted to the House. I do not wish it to be understood that the committee was absolutely wedded to the provisions of this Bill, although those provisions commended themselves to their judgment. We placed the Bill before the House, of course expecting that it will be considered, and we are quite open to receive any suggestions. The first section of the proposed Bill repeals or amends section 61 of the Dominion Elections Act, which is a section which provides the oath to be administered in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, there being special provisions for the method of carrying on an
election in these provinces. The substantial effect of this clause is that the provisions of section 62, in so far as the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta are concerned, are repealed, and it is the repeal of those sections that leads to the other provisions that are contained in this particular section. Under the section repealed there is a provision whereby a voter presenting himself at the poll, even although his name be not upon the lists that have been prepared by enumerators under the special provisions for those provinces, may he sworn by the deputy returning officer as to his qualifications, and may, upon his swearing' to his qualifications, be permitted to vote. The present provision would repeal that, and the consequence of repealing that necessitates an alteration in the oath to be administered to the voter in those provinces, making applicable the oath administered in other provinces where there is no such provision.

It does not repeal this, it only amends it by providing what oath may be administered.
Mr. DOHERTY, So far as the oath is concerned, it is amended by providing that the oath that may be put to these persons by reason of the fact that there was a provision that a man might be allowed to vote on his merely taking an oath of his qualifications, not being on a list at all, being repealed, then, instead of prescribing the oath "x", which is the oath of qualification, the prescription is that he shall take the usual oath as taken in the other provinces; but the provision of the Act under which he may be allowed to vote, although on no list, merely by taking an oath that he is a qualified person, is repealed.
What section repeals that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Section 62 is amended by striking out "provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta." Section 62, as it reads now, provides that in the Yukon territory and in the provinces of Saskatchewan, and Alberta, a man will be allowed to present himsell and to vote upon taking the oath of qualification. We repeal it as regards the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta by striking out of that section the words "the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan," leaving the provision standing, but only as applicable to the Yukon territories.

In repealing those
clauses as they apply to Saskatchewan and Alberta, is it the intention of the Govern-

ment to adopt the provincial list in connection with Dominion elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no provision in the Bill altering the other provisions of the Act as they now stand.
Is the report of the committee making the recommendations upon which the Bill is founded a unanimous report?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I explained before my colleague came in, while the committee was unanimous in submitting the Bill, we did not wish it to be understood that we were absolutely wedded to these provisions. We present them to the House with perfectly open minds as to any suggestions that may come as to their desirability. While I think the provisions commended themselves to the judgment of the committee, upon such examination as we were able to make and with such information as we had, we shall of course be glad to profit by the possibly greater knowledge of hon. gentlemen from the provinces concerned, who are certainly in a better position to judge of the conditions there than at least I should he.

I was one of the members of the special committee which had under consideration the Controverted Elections Act and the Dominion Elections Act. In considering the Controverted Elections Act it became necessary, of *course, to give some consideration to the Dominion Elections Act, and, as the minister has stated, the first three or four clauses were unanimously concurred m for presentation to the House. As the first two clauses of the Bill have oecas-sioned some little comment from hon. members from the Western provinces since being brought down to the House, I might say that these amendments came up accidently and incidentally, and we gave very little consideration to the matter indeed. During our consideration of the several clauses of the Dominion Elections Act, one member of the committee pointed out that in Alberta, Saskatchewan, and the Yukon, additions might be made to the electoral franchise list up to and including the very day of polling. Although I believe that is a provision of the Act, it was a revelation to me. It struck me as being an' absurd provision in these days, and particularly as regards the old provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, and I still say that it is a misfortune that such a provision should be in the Act. Further, I have since re-

cognized that we failed to give consideration to other sections of the Bill relative to the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and the Yukon territory. That is Part II of the Bill. Under the system of electoral registration prevailing in those two provinces and the Yukon, provision is made for the registration of electors, but they have to register within a period of eight days. There is a further provision that on election day any person claiming to be an elector may enroll and poll his vote upon taking the oath. When we were considering this Bill in the committee I myself was under the impression that these provisions were supplemental to the provincial e'ec-toral lists, or that there was a more comprehensive method of enrolling electors, and I was not sympathetic towards the continuance in the statute of a provision enabling electors to enroll on election day. I would consider that an unfortunate provision in the law of any country, unless there were very good reasons for it. Since my attention has been called to it, it is quite apparent to me that these amendments would be unfair in the circumstances, unless the provincial lists were adopted, or a more comprehensive system of enrolment of electors w.as contained in the statute. I think that the members of the committee failed to take that into consideration. I should very gladly vote for an amendment tp the Dominion Elections Act, if that could be done easily, making the provincial lists applicable for Dominion purposes, or adding further provisions providing for a longer time during which to enroll. But I recognize that in order to make both these amendments or either of them would take a great deal of time, and delay the Bill unduly. I would therefore suggest to the minister the withdrawal of sections 1, 2 and 3 of Bill 110. It is quite true that the committee were unanimous in recommending these sections to the House, and no one more than another was responsible for that. As soon as it was suggested I readily concurred, together with my colleague from Carleton (Mr. Car-veil), who was on the same committee. I do trust, however, that in the circumstances it will be agreeable to the minister to withdraw these provisions from the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As I understood it in
the committee, these sections were adopted principally by reason of the hearty approval of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and I think likewise of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell). *
With a slight reservation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Possibly. Personally
I confess I relied largely on their view of the matter. However, if it appears that those who come from the western provinces directly affected, and who are much more familiar with conditions there than I and the majority of the members of the committee pretend to be, look upon these provisions as undesirable, I would not for a moment insist on pressing the suggested amendment. I may point out that I do not think it would be proper to drop entirely the section, because part of its purpose was to amend an error that is evidently in the present statute, in so far as it refers to the oath that is to be taken by persons who are not on the list. Sec-ton 63 of the present Act provides:
Every person whose name is on the voters' list, unless sworn as in the next preceding section provided, shall before being permitted to vote, if required by any candidate, agent or elector, take the oath No. 1 in form Z.
On turning up oath No. 1 in form Z it will appear at once that what it was intended to say was oath No. 2 in form Z, and I think the statute ought to be amended so as to meet that requirement. Oath No. 1 in form Z is the oath that would be required of a person who was not upon the list at all, whereas evidently the oath that is intended is oath No. 2 form Z-the oath against bribery-because it is applicable to a man whose name is on the list. We retain that in any event. We do not interfere with the law which permits a man to swear his qualifications there and then. We are retaining section 62 of the Act, but subsection 2 of the Bill provides that section 62 is to be amended by substituting the word " two " for the word " one " in the fourth line thereof. The rest of that subsection might very well be dropped.
Would the minister please read the oath of the voter whose name is not on the list?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The oath to be taken
by the voter whose name is not on the list is as follows:
You do swear that you are of the male sex and a British subject, that you are not an Indian, you are of the full age of twenty-one years, and that you have resided in the province of Saskatchewan or Alberta or the Yukon territory (as the case may be) for at least twelve months, and (in case of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta) in this electoral district for at least three months, immediately preceding the issue of the writ of election, and 120
that you are now resident in this polling division, (the last ten words shall be omitted from the oath in the case of a person voting under section 59 or in Yukon territory.) So help me God.
That oath is intended to be taken by a person who, not being on the list, not having been enumerated, is allowed to vote because he swears that he has the necessary qualifications, whereas section 63 deals with the oath which is intended to be administered to the person whose name is on the voter's list. It is quite evident that it was intended by this section to require the person whose name is on the voter's list to take the oath that he was qualified to vote and that he had not received any money or reward for his vote. That oath, I think we ought to retain.

Speaking from memory, I think there is something in the general Act which provides that where a person has voted in the name of a voter, and the real voter comes along afterwards, the latter is entitled to vote. In that case the ballots are kept separate. May I ask the minister now how a case of that kind is dealt with in the West? Will the ballots of those persons who tendered their votes under these circumstances be placed in the box with the other ballots or will they be placed in a separate envelope?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it is possible for that situation to arise. There is a provision under which track can be kept of two men each claiming to be the voter whose name is on the list. However, in this case the question does not arise of one man trying to represent that he is another man and therefore entitled to vote. The man whose name is not on the list simply takes the oath that he is entitled to vote.
Ten or twenty men might go to a polling place, take the oath and vote whether their names were on the list or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

There was at one time
such an Act in the unorganized district of Ontario but time proved that it was rather a bad Act and it was elminated from the statutes.

I would imagine that if the proposed amendment to the Act as applied to Saskatchewan and Alberta were withdrawn section 63a in the new Bill would also have to be either withdrawn or amended. I think that was the question



that the minister was speaking to. There is evidently a mistake in the law as it reads. This was all threshed out in the committee but it will be made plain to any hon. gentleman who will follow the section as it is. In the Elections Act there is a particular part called part two which applies to Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Yukon Territory. Sections 31 to 65 apply exclusively to these provinces and this territory. Section 61 provides for the oath which may be administered in these two provinces and reference to form Z is in two parts. Part 1 is the oath that a person must take who claims to have the right to vote because he is a resident. That is the man who was referred to by the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) a few moments ago. A man comes up and says I am a resident of Alberta, I have been here for a year, or whatever time may be required, my name is not on the list and I demand the right to vote. Then he would take what is called oath No. 1 in form Z. Then, if some other person wants to challenge him on the ground that he has been guilty of bribery, he takes oath No. 2 in form Z. Oath No. 2 in form Z is practically the same as the general oath in form Y. If you abolished the right of a man to swear in his vo^e you would abolish the whole of form Z and bring him under the general law by which a man might be called upon to take the bribery oath as prescribed in form Y. If you go back to the original condition of affairs you must leave in form Z. But there is a mistake made in section 63 because it says:
Every person whose name is on the voters' list, unless sworn as in the next preceding section provided, shall before being permitted to vote, if required by any candidate, agent or elector, take the oath number one in Form Z.
If a man's name is on the list he should not be required to take the oath No. 1 because No. 1 is the oath which the man takes if his name is not on the list. I do not think that is what it was intended to provide for. The man whose name is on the list has the right to vote provided he takes the proper oath which is Form Z 2. lou would have to change the word " one " in the fourth i.ne of section 63 to the word " two " and then it would provide that the voter should take oath iNo. 2 instead of No. 1.
Mr. Mc(jRANEYT:	Suppose a name is
improperly on the enumerator's list as far as qualification goes, may the man not be challenged and may he not be required to take oath No. 1 as well as oath No. 2 ?
That was not our idea.

I think my hon. friend
the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. var-vell) are in error in imagining that there is a mistake in the present Act because there is none. You must remember that the list made in Saskatchewan and Alberta has nothing m common with the list you have in other parts of Canada. This is simply a pen, and ink list which is made after the proclamation has been issued and it must be posted up eight days before the election. Any man may go to the enumerator and ask to have his name put on. The enumerator as a rule does not swear that man or make any particular effort to satisfy himself that the man is entitled to vote and the name goes on the list whether the applicant is entitled to vote or not. Many a name is put on these individual lists. There is a special list for each polling division. In my own constituency last election there were 111 enumerators appointed. The idea of the oath is all right. Many names may be put on the list of persons who are not entitled or qualified to vote, men who may not be British subjects, may net have resided a year in the province .and may not have resided three months in the electoral district. It is very necessary to keep that oath as it is. If you want to provide further that, in addition to taking that oath of qualification, each voter who is not on the list, should also be sworn as to bribery, there is no objection as to that. That could be done as it is; but if it cannot be done, there will be no objection to having a man whose name is not on the list take both the oaths. I can quite understand my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and other members of the committee who are not from either Saskatchewan or Alberta not realizing what they were doing when they proposed to put in these amendments, which would put the elections simply into the hands of a large number of enumerators who might be good enumerators or who might be bad ones. I do not like the present system of making the lists that we have in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The time has come when there should be a better system. Those provinces are old enough and settled up enough now to have the same system as is followed in the other provinces. It is very awkward for a candidate to come up on the day of an election and have no idea as to who is on the voters' list. If you are to do away with the right of a man to vote by coming up on election day and putting his

name on the list, then you must have a proper provision for the making of the list and the revision of the list. There is at present no provision for the revision of the list by the enumerator at each polling division.
Yes, there is.

I beg your pardon. Any one can go to an enumerator and ask him to put on or to take off certain names, but he does not need to do so. Until you have a proper list, of which there would be a proper revision, you must leave in the statute that provision by which a bona fide voter, who is perfectly entitled to vote but whose name is left off the pen and ink list inadvertently or by design, may go up on election day take the oath that he is qualified and that he has not been bribed, and register his vote.
Is there any provincial list?
There is a provincial list in the province of Saskatchewan, but not in the province of Alberta.

The hon. member for Assinitooia contends that under section 62 new names may be added to the voter's lists up to and including election day. Before a vote is registered, the oath must be put to the voter under section 63.
Yes.

The proposed
change in this Act was probably made by the committee in consequence of certain conditions that I pointed out to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) and subsequently to the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). During all the elections that I have seen in western Canada-and they have all been conducted under the auspices of hon. gentlemen opposite-the conditions now imposed by the statute have tended to two things: first, to a limitation of the exercise of the franchise by those who should exercise it, and, secondly, to corruption of the worst type. The hon. member for Carleton, N.B., was very much impressed with the fact when I went over the Act and showed it to him, and for that matter so was the hon. junior member for Halifax. I then directed the attention of the committee to the matter without having consulted any of my colleagues on this side of the House, and without having discussed it with them in any way, shape or form. I have said frequently in elections 120*
that have 'been held in the West that, if I ever had an opportunity, I would endeavour, so far as I could, to have a list prepared that would be a final list upon which an election might be held. The primary reason for that was that I had observed during all the elections that were held while I was in the West, numbers of men brought in from the outside, in many instances gangs of workmen on railways and in some instances other men, taken to the polls, sworn in and their ballots put into the box, although their names were not on the list. They left immediately . after having voted, and to know exactly where they resided would be a somewhat difficult proposition. That condition of affairs grew up in the West, because in the first instance, as in all other unorganized territories, all that was necessary for a man to do to enable him to vote was to go up and swear his-vote in. In the early days in the Northwest Territories, all a man had to do was to swear that he had lived twelve months in the Northwest Territories and three months in the particular electoral district, and his ballot was put into the box and he went away. I will give a well-known case. It occurred before I went West, but it has been authenticated. Certain people gathered together a couple of hundred men and they voted them four times at four different polls. This happened before 1896. They put the men on a train and took them to one poll and voted them there. Then they put them on the train again and took them to another poll and voted them there, and so on, so that there were between 700 and 800 votes polled at four different places, but the voters were all the same 200 men. All they had to do was to swear their votes in and drop their ballots into the box. In due Lime enumerators were appointed. My hon. friend from Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is wrong in his statement. The enumerators do sit as a court of revision. Under the law as it now stands, as soon as a writ is issued, the returning officer under certain conditions appoints enumerators; but if he does not do that, prior to the date of the issue of the writ, the Governor in Council may appoint enumerators. An enumerator may sit for one polling division or for three or four. What is his duty? Before commencing to discharge it, he has to take an oath that he will do his duty, and put on the list the name of every person in his polling district who has lived twelve months, say in the province of Al-

berta and three months in the electoral district. He is then compelled to post up a copy of the list in the post office and to put at the foot of it a notice saying that he will sit two hours a day, naming the time and the place, for the purpose of revising the list. He must certify to that list and send it to the returning officer for the district before the hour of eight o'clock on the morning of the election, in order that it may be completed. I think it was not the immediate predecessor of the present Minister of Justice who put section 65 into the Act. Section 65 reads:
Every voter shall be entitled to vote, whose name is on the voters' list and has not been erased therefrom, in accordance with the foregoing provisions of this Part.
In other words, as the law now stands, the list itself is to be taken as conclusive proof of the voter's right to vote. That section was put upon the Statute Book, I think, about 1903 or 1904. As regards this provision there is no man living in the West, who desires to have a clean, decent election who does not know that it means just the opposite of a clean, decent election. I appeal to my hon. friend for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). Has he not seen many men brought in to a district' and kept at a hotel overnight and taken up to a polling station next day and voted? That is a bad thing for the body politic and a bad thing for democracy. I directed the attention of the hon. member for Carleton and the hon. junior member for Halifax to these provisions, and they thought it wrong to have such provisions as those in the Statute Book.
Later, in consequence of what was said to them by their fellow-members from western Canada as to the inadequacy of proper revision of the list by enumerators without right of appeal to a district court or other judge, they felt they were doing an injustice to their friends from the West. So I say, as I said in the committee, I am not pressing it. If it is felt that it will work an injustice, and if it will prevent any man from having a vote who ought to vote, I am content that it should be withdrawn. But I do say this Parliament should not permit a Franchise Act of this kind to stand upon the statute book.

Not any longer
than we can help.

No. The right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has asked' whether there is a list. In Saskatche-

wan they have a provincial list. Alberta ever since the year after it became a province has had provision for a list, but the * law was not to come into force until after proclamation issued, and year after year no proclamation has issued. There could not be anything in election processes more disgraceful than that which takes place in a provincial election under the present law. There is an enumerator for each polling place, and members can imagine what takes place in a local or Dominion election. Writs are issued and a returning officer is appointed. That returning officer is immediately surrounded by the hungry seekers for some sort of office, and I am not speaking of one side more than of another. These people want to be appointed enumerators, and each presses his claim. Very often the man appointed is a violent partisan. He is the enumerator for a little district in which there are perhaps two hundred voters. He takes the oath of office, and very often proceeds to put on his list as many Liberals or as many Conservatives, according to his partisan leanings, as he can find. In my last election, by reason of that, I had to employ and pay a very large number of men to go from house to house throughout the city of Calgary to get the names of the whole population, and then go to the enumerators and see that the names that had been left off were put on. When I tell you that my own name was left off you will understand to what extremes this leaving off is carried. That may have been an accident, but I am stating what happened. Then, if in addition, you have a railroad gang brought in from British Columbia, after they have polled their votes there, to come to some particular poll in Alberta and vote there, as has been done-swearing in their votes and next morning being in British Columbia so that any attempt to pursue them for perjury-is utterly futile-you will see that conditions are bad.
One word more. In section 63 of the Act it is provided that the electors shall take oath No. 1 under form Z. Having regard to the provisions of 62 and 65-I have read 65-it is apparent that sections 62, 63 -and 65 are not consistent with one another. Originally, we started to make that little -change, and when the discussion took place we arrived at the conclusion that it would be wise to prevent them from swearing in their votes, a provision which is now not to be proceeded with. We shall never have proper elections in Alberta unless we get a decent election

law in the province. I was only seeking to show that in their anxiety to pass section 65, the committee omitted to make the amendments necessary to make sections 62, 63 and 65 consistent. Leave the law as it is and you will have an election on the same conditions as before, much as I regret it.

Does the hon. gentleman say that it is necessary to amend section 63 now? I wish to call his attention to the fact that apparently that section is to provide a penalty for refusing to take the oath of qualification when put to the voter.

I do not say that it is going to make a very great difference. But sections 62, 63 and 65, read with section 61, show some little inconsistency, although I think it can be worked out in practice as it has been in the past.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me under which sections he finds provision made for the proper revision of the list?

There are two. Section 48 reads:
Each such enumerator shall complete, date at his place of residence, and sign the copies of the voters' list or lists as aforesaid, in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, eight days before the polling day... .
In either of the said provinces, one of the places where copies of the lists are to be so posted up shall be the post office nearest to the place appointed as the polling station for the polling subdivision, or, if there is no such post office, a conspicuous place outside and adjoining the main entrance to such polling station.
That is the provision about revision of the lists.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section I-repealing provision to enable person not on list to vote in Saskatchewan and Alberta and making form Y apply to those provinces:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that the Bill be amended by striking out section 1.

Motion agreed to.
On section 2-changing list of places in which deferred elections may be held:

I move that this Bill be amended by inserting therein the following as section 1:
1. Section 70 of the Dominion Election Act, chapter 6 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, is amended by adding thereto the following subsection :
(h) Any person during the time he is a director of or holds, either directly or indirectly, a controlling interest in any incorporated company having a contract or agreement, expressed or implied, or any unsatisfied claim arising therefrom, with or for or against the Government of Canada on behalf of the Crown, or with or for or against any of the officers of the Government of Canada for which any public money of Canada is to be paid.
Paragraph (d) of section 70 of the Dominion Elections Act says:
Every person directly or indirectly, alone or with any other person, by himself or by the interposition of any trustee or third party, holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing any contract or agreement, express or implied, with or for the Government of Canada, on behalf of the Crown, or with or for any of the officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, during the time he is so holding or enjoying, undertaking or executing.
