Any person, therefore, having a contract with the Government, is ineligible as a candidate for election to the House of Commons, but he may be a shareholder or have a controlling interest in an incorporated company which has a contract with the Government, and still be eligible for election. When the Elections Act was first passed, business was not carried on. as it is to-day. There were very few incorporated companies then, but now business is carried on mostly by joint stock companies.

Is this proposed
amendment part of the Bill which the hon. member introduced a few days ago?
Yes.
Then I submit that the hon. gentleman is out of order in moving an amendment which embodies provisions contained in a Bill already on the Order Paper.

If the hon. Minister of
Justice wants to adopt my amendment, I shall be glad to hand it over to him, or I can have the order discharged for the second reading of the Bill standing in my name. I do not think the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) should take advantage of a technicality in order to rule out an amendment which I think is a proper one.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the point of OTder raised by the hon. member for Halton is well taken, because the hon. member for Prescott admits that there is on the Order

Paper a measure standing in his name, which is the same as the amendment which he proposes to this Bill.
There is a provision in the Senate and House of Commons Act which secures the independence of members of this House; I think the independence of candidates for elections should be secured also.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not understand that in the Senate and House of Commons Act there is at the present time any provision analogous to the provision which the hon. gentleman wants to introduce into this Bill.

A few days ago I presented the Bill standing in my name, but as hon. gentlemen opposite have control of the proceedings of this House I suppose it will be impossible for my Bill to reach its second reading this session. In order to put this provision into effect, however, the Elections Act could be amended first, and the Senate and House of Commons Act afterwards. I would point out that the hon. Minister of Justice adopted the principle of two Bills, in the names of the hon. member for Guys-borough and the hon. member for Saskatoon respectively, having in view an amendment of the Criminal Code, while these Bills were on the Order Paper.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member is mistaken in that respect. The two Bills to which he refers were referred to a special committee to consider proposed amendments to the Criminal Code, and they came back inserted in a Bill which that committee reported to the House as the result of their deliberations. In this case we are dealing with a Bill that 'has been reported by a special committee also, and I do not at the moment quite see how I can come to the assistance of the 'hon. gentleman in what he is endeavouring to do. If he is out of order in proposing this amendment, I should be equally out of order in supporting it. The other Bill, which he says is the same as the proposed amendment, being on the Order Paper, and the Chairman having ruled that that puts this proposal out of order, I do not very well see how I can remedy the situation.

It could be remedied in this way; before this Bill is read the third time, the order for the second reading of the Bill standing in my name could be discharged.
[The Chairman.]

The Chairman has ruled that this amendment is out of order. I am not prepared to say that the ruling is wrong, but I suggest to the hon. member for Prescott that he look the matter up and, if he is right, then he can move his amendment on the third reading of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps it might be well for us all to accept the suggestion of the right hon. gentleman and look into it more fully.
Then the hon. minister will not press the third reading of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. The second section is rendered necessary by the fact that the Representation Act has changed the designations of certain constituencies. Under the Elections Act as it now stands, the constituencies of Comox-Atlin, Kootenay and Yale-Cariboo are enumerated among those constituencies in which elections may be deferred, These three constituencies have been subdivided so as to each form two constituencies. It is not proposed that in all of these new constituencies deferred elections may be held, but simply in three of them, Skeena, West Kootenay and Cariboo.
It did not appear to me to be necessary to have a deferred election in the old constituency of Kootenay. Then why is it necessary in West Kootenay?

West Kootenay includes the Big Bend country, away to the north of Revelstoke and Golden, where it is difficult to get about, and it was probably that part of the old district that made it necessary to have a deferred election in Kootenay. Of course the conditions have not changed in that respect in West Kootenay.
Are the three constituencies named the only three in the Dominion in which there may be deferred elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No; under section 86 there may be deferred elections also in Chicoutimi and Saguenay, and Gaspe, in the province of Quebec.
On Section 3-extending provision re death of candidates to Alberta and Saskatchewan :
Why is that necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose is to
assimilate the law in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan to the law as it prevails throughout the rest of the Dominion, in the event of a candidate dying

after nomination and before the close of the polls.

Did the committee give any consideration to the case of Gaspe? Mr. Monk, the late member for Jacques Cartier in this House, gave many facts in support of bringing Gaspe in line with other constituencies. Gaspe now has railway communication, and for the provincial election of 1897, when I had the honour of being a candidate, the nomination was made a month earlier, but the vote was taken on the same day as in the rest of the province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have to admit that the question of Gaspe did not come before the committee. As I pointed out, the way in which the question presented itself to us was that we were bound to do something to make the description of the British Columbia constituencies correspond with their new boundaries, and we found it was not necessary to defer the elections in the whole six. It was not suggested to us that there was any change in conditions in Gaspe from those which prevailed when the present law was enacted.	,

The conditions are very much changed there. We have a daily train service right down to Gaspe Basin, and there is now telegraphic communication with the Magdalen islands. There is provision in the law for a telegraphic proclamation. But if the committee have not considered the matter I would not be prepared to make a suggestion.
On Section 4-hours of polling extended- 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.:

In so far as the rural constituency of Quebec are concerned, this change is not at all necessary. By five o'clock all the votes have been cast, and I have heard members from Nova Scotia say that election day is the longest day in the year.

I want to endorse what has been said toy the hon. member (Mt. Marcil). It may be advisable to extend the hours in the cities, but I certainly think they should not be extended in the rural districts. The hon. member for Bona-veature (Mr. Marcil) has expressed my views precisely.

In justice to the special committee, I must say that this clause, as printed, is really not the recommendation of the committee. During the sittings of the committee, we were approached .by representatives of railway organizations, who asked us to make amendments to the Dominion Elections Act, if it were possible, whereby greater facilities tor voting could be afforded to that class of electors. Many suggestions were made and considered, tout the committee found difficulties attaching to them all. We did consider last session the propriety of affording railway men an opportunity to vote during 24 or 48 hours preceding the day of polling. The idea was that polling booths should be placed at divisional points, hut eventually we considered that impracticable. We also considered the suggestion of having the polling booths in cities open for a greater number of hours than is now provided by statute. There were difficulties connected with that suggestion too, although it might possibly be worked out. Then it was thought that we might meet the requests of a great number of railway voters by extending the hours of voting from eight in the morning until a later hour than five in the afternoon. The committee were not at all agreed upon the matter, and at last we concluded to put this section in the Bill, leaving it open to the House to consider. So this clause is not the recommendation of the committee, hut was put in more for the purpose of securing an expression of opinion from the House generally as to What should be done.

In what way would it
assist railway men to extend the hours from eight in the morning .until after five in the evening? It is very seldom that any votes to speak of are polled in the small cities after four o'clock. In towns like that in which I live, we generally have the vote all polled before five o'clock.

I think this provision
will be a good thing in certain parts of the country. For instance, workingmen may work during the noon hour and get off an hour earlier in the evening. If they got off at five o'clock they would be able to vote between five and six. I .think that would accommodate a certain number of people.

I was one of
those who. appeared before the committee and suggested this, or some similar amendment. When we look at our law, we find that in the matter of polling we are very many years behind every other country situated as we are, especially as regards affording facilities to the people who live in cities or urban districts to poll their votes. Our law in that respect has never been changed, and the hours have always been

from nine in the morning until five at night. Other countries have responded to the requirements of civilization in congested districts, and extended the polling hours so as to give everybody a fair opportunity to poll his vote. Those who have ample time under the present law to poll their votes, should have regard to other people differently situated in different parts of the country, and should be willing to let the polls remain open an hour or two longer than they themselves need, in order to give their fellow citizens an opportunity of polling. England, in 1872, changed the hours to from eight in the morning until eight at night, and that is still the law in England. I have at some trouble gone through, the legislation of all the states of the American Union and I think they are almost uniform in keeping the polls open for about that length of time. Australia, since 1903, has had the polls open from eight in the morning until eight at night. There is not only the difficulty about polling votes, but a more far-reaching difficulty than that. I think one-half of the corruption that takes place during an election in a city district is due to the endeavour to poll the vote between the hours at present assigned. To-day, the polls open at nine in the morning; but long before that hour mechanics and artisans, and all working people in fact, are at their work. The ordinary business man, the clerk in the bank or in the insurance office, all the assistants in the 'down town offices are at work by nine or thereabouts. We must not forget that to-day the urban population of Canada is very large, and I submit that those who are living in country districts should give their fellow-citizens in the cities an opportunity to poll their votes. Under the usual provincial law, a man votes in the district where he sleeps. In the city of Toronto, for instance-and I do not desire to parade Toronto before this House particularly-the great majority of people reside anywhere from two to four or six miles away from their work, and consequently have to leave their homes, close to which they vote, half an hour before they wish to arrive at tKeir place of work. The result is that when the polls open many people have left their homes and gone to work, for they do not desire to lose part of the day, and those who go to the polls see this spectacle: ten, fifteen or thirty men lined up outside the booth, waiting on the convenience of the deputy returning officer, who does not let them in until nine. Are elections held for the 
convenience of the people or for the convenience of the deputy returning officer? I think the time has come when the polling booths in cities should be open from eight in the morning until eight at night. The ordinary man does not leave fils work before five oclock, the working-man at all events, and at five the polls close. If the man is going to get in his vote, he has to rush back to the neighborhood in which he lives, and that takes some time. That is the condition in Toronto and other cities throughout Canada, and I leave it to the judgment of the House whether I am correct or not. In thickly-congested districts, there is one rush to get the vote out. In large cities there is a line of motor-cars waiting at the factory doors to carry voters to the polls. We can form our own opinion whether these are all volunteers or not, but there they are, waiting to take the voters to tne polls, and all sorts of influence is used with the proprietors of factories to get them to let some of their men out and to keep some of them in, according to what their political complexion is supposed to be.
Take the example that was mentioned by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Railway people, commercial travellers and men of that kind are given no opportunty in the morning to poll their votes because they are put on trains, they have to go outside and make their daily runs, they do not, as a rule, come back until after five o'clock, and then the polls are closed against them. An election only takes place one in three, four or five years. Every civilized country I know of keeps the polls open very much longer than we do here. The present condition is wholly unsuited to cities. It leads to corruption, it leads to the bribing of men to go to the polls or to remain away, and tends very greatly to increase the corruption arising from the employing of teams and vehicles to drive men to the polls. The matter contained in this amendment is a subject that I have introduced in this House on many occasions. I have not succeeded in accomplishing anything as yet, but as the country grows, and as we find city people becoming the higher percentage of the whole, so grows the need of legislation of this kind. It has been asked for by the labouring classes of Canada. I do not want to burden people who do not want the polls kept open until later. It might be arranged by the committee that in rural districts the polls shall remain open during the present hours,

but that as far as cities are concerned, and ridings of which cities form a part, the polls should be kept open at least from eight in the morning until six at night. These hours are short enough. In the Old Country they find it necessary to close the polls at eight o'clock at night, but as recently as 1913 an amendment was made in the . election law extending the time for closing the polls to nine o'clock at night if either candidate or his agent so asks. It is found there that even eight o'clock is not long enough, and the polls are to remain open from seven a.m. until nine p.m. if either candidate or his agent asks for it.
Where is that?

Chapter 6, Imperial
Acts, 1913. Since 1872 they have had the polls open from eight in the morning until eight at night. In 1913 they passed an amendment permitting either candidate to request that the polls be opened at seven o'clock and be kept open until nine o'clock at night, showing the growth and tendency of the present age to offer every facility for a man to poll his vote. I think there is nothing more that I could say that would be new on the subject. The matter is before the committee. As I say, this change is needed in cities. If our friends in the rural districts do not want this amendment to the Act, doubtless the committee might think it well to permit the polls in the rural districts to remain open in accordance with the present hours and to remain open in cities at least from eight to six.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman tell the committee if in Australia they have plural voting?
They have proportional representation and several classes of voting there.

The riding from which I come has a very large railway vote and the inadequacy of the present law to enable the railway vote to be polled has repeatedly been brought to my attention. I certainly am in favour of the extension of the hours of polling. If I could make a suggestion based on my experience, it would be to open the poll as early as six o'clock in the morning in these districts even if it were closed somewhat earlier in the evening. If the poll were opened in cities at six o'clock in the morning voters could go to the poll before going to the work. Another thing that I think would ease the
situation is this: Saturday is becoming more and more a public holiday in this country especially for artisans and those who work in factories. If we had the election on Saturday or Monday the great bulk of the voters made up of commercial travellers would get their votes recorded. Many of them now miss the opportunity of voting. They are very sore about that and they have repeatedly called public attention to the fact that they are - deprived of their vote. Another thing that could be done would be for the Railway Commission to take charge of the running of all trains,-perhaps some passenger trains-delay them for an hour at the point of starting, and allow the men who wish to do so to vote. In that way a great many votes might be recorded. We must do something in the way of giving these people who are not able to vote now an opportunity to vote. The selection of Saturday-Saturday preferably-or Monday, as the day of voting would do a great deal to remove the present inconvenience. There is no reason why election day should not be the most sacred day in this country. I admire what the French people do in making the recording of their votes practically a religious duty with the people and they vote on Sunday because every person has an opportunity of voting on that day. It might not suit the genius of our people here to have a law such as that but it would be in the line of progress and in line with what they are doing in other countries if we had at least a half holiday on election day and in cities the most convenient day for that half holiday would be Saturday or Monday. If we laid down the principle that we would have our election day either on Saturday or Monday a great many railway men and commercial travellers would . have an opportunity of voting for they could go to the polls early in the morning and record their votes.
Would my hon. friend delay trains an hour?
Yes.
Passenger trains?

I did not say passenger trains. I said that I would like the railway commission to take charge of divisional points, and the despatch of freight trains from divisional points and delay them probably for an hour or hasten them so that the men would get their votes polled. It is easy to speed up trains, it is often done and the men would get their votes

polled in that way. But the biggest relief, without any great widening of the law, would he to open earlier in the morning and have the election on Saturday preferably to any other day in the week. It is now largely a half holiday and if we had the election on Saturday the people could go to the polls and have their votes recorded. It is the desire of a great many people to see a change in the law inasmuch as they now lose their votes. Anybody who has been identified with elections, and who has taken part in them, must see that, especially in the larger cities, there is a substantial grievance among large sections of the voters that they are not able to record their votes because of the limited time in which the polls are open, and also the inconvenience caused by the particular day selected.

I think it will be a surprise to most of the members of this House that any suggestion should be made to extend the hours of polling in rural districts. For my part, I have had some experience in elections and I do not recollect one suggestion from any voter in a rural district that the time should be extended for the opening or closing of the polls. I think a good deal can be said, and already a good deal has been submitted to the committee for consideration, in favour of the proposition that in the larger cities, such as Montreal, Toronto, and possibly other cities in the Dominion, longer hours for polling would be better but for the great mass of the constituencies, which are rural constituencies. I do not think that there has been any suggestion by any of the rural members in support of a proposal of this kind and I was very glad to learn from the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) that this was not the matured judgment of the committee, but rather that they were reporting it to the House for its consideration. I would be disposed to think that if such a change in the law were made universal in Canada, applying it to rural districts as well as to cities, the people would be very much opposed to it and feel that it would be a change for the worse rather than for the better.

As I was a member of the committee, perhaps it might be wise for me to give this committee some idea of the many propositions brought before us from time to time. Many claims were advocated, especially by railway men. We had representations from, ' I think, the Trades and

Labour Council, or at any rate, some body representing railway men, and they presented this proposition in a very strong light. There was a proposal that we open the divisional points the day before an election. I was very sorry the committee did not see its way clear to accept that proposition and work it out. Possibly my personal experience may have led me to be particularly sympathetic along that line, because I had the unpleasant experience of seeing many men put out of my constituency on election day, so that it was impossible for them to register their vote. Possibly other hon. members here have had a like experience. A large number of railway men are not able to cast their votes on election day. It was suggested that, if a box could be arranged for at each divisional point and kept open from noon of the day prior to the election until the close of the election, 90 per cent of the railway men would have the right to vote. An objection was raised to that. Suppose you had only a dozen railway votes at a particular railway point, and the majority voted one way, you would eliminate the idea of secrecy of the ballot. The railway men themselves, however, did not consider that an objection. They were willing to accept all the burdens provided that they had the right to vote.
In justice to myself I may say that I was not able to be present at the last three or four sittings of the committee, being engaged on other committees. The last time I was present at a meeting of this committee, a suggestion was made that seemed a very reasonable one. It was that there should be a provision that the Governor in Council shoulu nave the power to decide whether or not the hour should be extended from six o'clock in the morning until eight o'clock in the evening in all cities of Canada having a population of a given amount, I think 100,000.
And railway divisional points.

I am told that the committee at a later session turned that suggestion down, because they felt that in some way the Governor in Council might be charged with not exercising the best discretion. It was perhaps putting an unfair discretion on tire Governor in Council.
I could not see any harm in that suggestion, because it would give Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver the right to take advantage of that provision. If 100,000 ' was thought too great, the minimum might

be lowered to 75,000. We also discussed the question of giving the right to towns of 50,000; but there are a great many towns in Canada which have a population of 50,000 and which also have country districts incorporated with the cities. Take the city and county of St. John. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) knows that in his constituency there are voters living very nearly 100 miles away from the city of St. John. In the county of Halifax there are voters living some forty or fifty miles away from the city. Therefore we found difficulties in all those cases. It seems to me that some scheme might be worked out by placing the limit at 75,000, and giving the Governor in Council the right to state the electoral districts in which the hours of polling should be extended. I am very much in sympathy with the statement put forward by my hon. friend the member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell), because from my experience of a little town of 4,000 or 5,000, I can quite realize the difficulty of polling a vote in a large city. I can also realize some of the expense entailed on candidates and committee men in getting people from great distances to the polling stations. That difficulty is obviated to some extent in section 5, which reads as follows:
Every employer shall on polling day give every voter in his employ at least one additional hour for voting other than the noon hour.
That would get around the difficulty to some extent, but still I realize that it does not obviate the difficulty altogether, and that there is a great rush to try to poll the labour vote in big districts within the prescribed time. We discussed another proposition, that in all the cities of say 25,000 or 30,000 or 40,000 or upwards, we might extend the time of polling in the city portion of the constituency to seven or eight o'clock, and allow the country portion of the constituency to close its polls at five, as at present.

Hear, hear.
Mr. CARVELL; My hon. friend says "hear, hear"; but let us argue the other side of the question. Let us take the city of Halifax as an illustration. The poll closes at five o'clock. There are telephones throughout the country. The consequence will be that at six o'clock you will know the results of the polling in the whole county of Halifax, and we shall say it is a tie or practically a tie, and that there is one or two hours left to poll the remainder
of the votes. The number of votes left would not be very great, and we were afraid -and it is the experience of every man here, and we have all had experience of elections-that there might be redoubled efforts on the part of committee men to poll the votes in the last hour or two. All these matters were considered very carefully by the committee, and we could see some strong reasons against them all unless we made them general. I quite agree with the decision come to by the committee to make a recommendation to the House in order to bring the matter up for discussion; but, personally, I would like to see something done by which the Governor in Council would have the power to extend the time in big cities and allow the remainder of the districts, both rural and urban, to vote within the prescribed hours as at present provided. Certainly in all rural constituencies from eight o'clock in the morning until five o'clock in the afternoon is ample time. In some cases the people, long before five o'clock, are waiting for the hour to come.	-

My instructions are quite different, and they are to ask for an extension of the hours for polling. I listened to the discussion with a great deal of interest, in fact, I might say, curiosity, because I wished to find out the objections to the great general principle of extending the hours of polling and enlarging the opportunity of exercising the franchise. Surely it is incumbent upon those gentlemen who object to state forcibly and clearly why they wish to restrain the opportunity of the people to exercise the franchise.
We are not discussing an Act for the suppression of corruption, but an Act permitting the exercise of the franchise, and therefore it should be as wide as possible. I am amazed at the suggestion of the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). The Saturday holiday is earned by . the workingman who works an hour longer each day during the week in order to get it, and I have been told by workingmen that if I thought they were going to give up that half holiday for the purpose of electing any politician, I had another think coming. That seems entirely reasonable to me. I am grieved when I think of the personnel of this committee, that they were not able to hatch up something better than this Bill,

You are on the
committee yourself.
No.

You were called before
the committee.

That is different. It
seems to me that if we are in such a bad state in this country that we cannot allow an extended number of hours to the people -who, so far as I know, want that extension-in order that they may reasonably exercise their franchise, then we are in a bad state indeed, especially if we believe that the demon of corruption is going about like a roaring lion. If the railway people cannot vote becausp they cannot get to the ballot box, let us provide more ballot boxes, but to hang up these necessary reforms because of all sorts of little tupenny ha'penny objections seems to me inconsistent with the dignity of this House.

In the last elections held in the province of Ontario for the legislative assembly the polls were opened at eight o'clock and closed at five o'clock in the afternoon in cities of two hundred thousand population and over. That amendment was adopted, I understand, because of the growth' of Toronto, which is the only city in Ontario having a population of two hundred thousand. In this country, where our cities are growing up so rapidly, and where the desire of the people is to get out into the suburbs where they may have cheaper rentals, a great many people-clerks, labouring people, employers and others-live	at a distance
from the centre and must spend perhaps three-quarters of an hour or an hour in going from their place of occupation to the poll where their votes must be cast. I think the time has come when an exception ought to be made in respect of cities of say two hundred thousand population or over. I would not think it desirable to extend this to rural places; but in view of the great growth of our cities and of the precedents that have been read by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) of amendments to the election laws in other places, we might very well extend the time of polling in these cities by one hour in the morning. The request was made of me that I should advocate the keeping open of the polls until six o'clock instead of five, But I would not go so far as that even with respect to cities of two hundred thousand population. If a man could vote before he goes to his place of occupation in the morning and get there by, say ten o'clock, it would be a great convenience and many
[Hr. Burnham.]
more voters would cast their ballots than under the present system.

Does the hon. gentleman think that opening the poll at eight o'clock would be a benefit to the labouring man? I can understand how it would help clerks and others, but when it comes to the labouring man, I am afraid it would not be of much use to him.

In the section which follows it is provided that on polling day the employer is obliged to allow the employee an hour without deduction from 9 p.m. his wages. For the man whp does not start work until eight in the morning in the regular way, it seems to me it would be a great convenience to be able to vote before nine o'clock.

For many years there was great complaint on the part of the commercial travellers regarding the days chosen for elections. There are in the neighborhood of twenty-five thousand travellers in Canada, and probably twenty per cent of them lose the opportunity to exercise their franchise.
Mr. W. F. MACLEAN And they are the keenest politicians in the country.

Yes. It has been suggested to me that if Friday could be set apart as the day of polling it would be acceptable to the travellers. The light-sample men who carry grips leave their homes on Sunday so that they may get upon the territory they have to cover on Monday morning. As to heavy sample-men, with trunks, it does not make so much difference, b,ut they would work a little harder and a little later in order that they might get in on Friday to poll their votes. I am in accord with the hon. member for Toronto that if the polls were open at 7 o'clock, a.m., it would be of advantage to those who want to leave by an early train.

I quite agree with the views expressed by my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) that there has been no request from any part of the country to change the hours of polling in rural constituencies. I am rather at a loss to appreciate the argument of my hon. friend from South Toronto. It is urged that in large cities railway men and commercial travellers do not have a chance to vote, but I do not see that the proposition contained in this section offers any solution of this problem. If the commercial traveller is away from home the extension of the time of poll-

ing by an hour in the morning is of no use to him; if he is at home, he can vote as well between nine and five as he can between eight and six. So we can eliminate their case from those to be considered in this connection. As to the railway men, surely my hon friend from South York will agree that his proposal that trains be stopped to allow railway men to vote is impracticable. You cannot work out a law in regard to the operation of voting that is going to satisfy everybody. There must always be some people who have to work on that day. The idea is to have as few people as possible deprived of their franchise. The proposal of the hon. member would stand in the way of those who desire to use the trains to reach their polling places. A man may have come hundreds of miles to vote in his home constituency only to find that by reason of the dislocation of the train service through delaying trains for an hour in the morning he could not reach the poll at all. During elections the movement of voters in the country is very great, and the prompt arrival and departure of trains is of great importance. By reason of delay or disarrangement of train services, a great many people might be unable to reach the polls before they close.

My suggestion
was with regard to freight trains starting from divisional points, where the bulk of the voters live.

After all, the idea is to reduce to the minimum the number of persons who are deprived of the privilege of voting. I do not believe that public sentiment favours a wholesale change in the law. In Nova Scotia-I speak of provincial elections-the polls open at eight o'clock in the morning and close at five in the afternoon; it has never been complained that the polls are not open as long as they should be. There are many railway men whose regular rounds take them from one divisional point to another point perhaps 100 miles distant, and unless the whole system of voting 'is disarranged, there is no way in which these men can be given an opportunity to vote. Certain people must of necessity, therefore, be debarred from the franchise. I do not say that in the case of cities the conditions could not be improved by lengthened hours of polling, but we must not confuse that phase of the matter with the proposal contained in this section, which, although put forward as a remedy, is really not a remedy for these conditions. Two hundred
men can vote at any polling subdivision with the greatest ease, provided they live anywhere within ten miles of the poll. If this is done, and if every employer is required to give his employees an hour to vote, it does seem to me that whatever practical difficulties there are will be obviated. I would not favour extending the hours of polling in rural constituencies past five o'clock. The experience has been that in general elections every vote is polled in rural constituencies long before five o'clock. It is my opinion that if the polls were kept open longer, the door would be opened to drunkenness and corruption. My hon. friend's suggestion about the English election laws is not apropos of the case. In England there is no simultaneous polling.
Practically so.

Not at all; a general election in Great Britain occupies a long period of time. Only one or two constituencies vote in the same day. If simultaneous polling is good, then Great Britain is very much behind us in that respect.
I do not quite catch my hon. friend's meaning. What bearing has the question of simultaneous polling upon the hours of voting?

I was simply discussing whether we should go to Great Britain for instruction as to how to run elections. I was suggesting that because they have simultaneous polling over there, which most people regaid as a rather retrograde condition, they are not ahead of us in this matter. Another consideration is the crowded population of the British Isles, which gives rise to a condition entirely different from that which exists in this country, comprised, as it is, of huge areas of land and a scattered population. Then again, take the conditions that exist in Great Britain in reference to the counting of the votes. Would it be practicable in this country to take all the ballot boxes from the country districts, bring them to a central place, and there count the ballots? They do that in England, and I hardly think it would be suggested that we should do that here. This only goes to show that in matters of this kind the peculiar conditions of the country concerned must be carefully considered. I do submit that there is no crying need for any radical change in the present law. Anomalies do exist, and, perhaps, can be remedied to a

certain extent, but the minority must always give way to the majority in the matter of convenience and the public interest. Personally, I would support no change in the law except the proposal to have the polls open at eight o'clock in the morning.

Representing *a rural constituency, I am opposed to any further discrimination in the matter of the franchise as between rural and urban municipalities. There is a distinction in the matter of registration in favour of the cities that is, to some extent, objectionable. The difficulty in connection with this whole matter is not so much with reference to the hours for voting, because cities, no matter how large, are subdivided into a certain number of polling subdivisions, just as the rural sections are, and if the employer assumes an attitude of fairness towards his employees and gives them an opportunity to vote, the conditions are quite in favour of their being able to register their vote. I think the best solution of the difficulty would be to provide for a half-holiday, or at least a quarter-holiday, and thus put the voter in a position where he will be absolutely untrammelled by any restrictions in the matter of exercising his franchise. It is my experience that while many employers of labour are willing to allow their employees who are favourable to their views to exercise their franchise, a veiled threat is held out to those who are not favourable to the employer's political views that if they do exercise the franchise they take the consequences upon themselves. The extra hour is absolutely of no use to the workingman where his employer wants to put restrictions on him.
Why? It is the law of the land.
I know it is the law of the land, but the man is afraid to go out to exercise his franchise.
Oh, no.

I know it, I know it from personal observation. My reason for speaking of this is that I think the section following this is very closely related to the present one. It is not so much the extra hour for polling that is important as to have a fixed time when employees shall have the right to go untrammelled to exercise that franchise. It is suggested that a certain number of men be allowed to go at one hour and a certain number at another hour in order not to inconvenience the

management of the factory. I would favour having the hours for voting, if 8 o'clock is too early, from 9 until 6 p.m. I would approve of the extra hour at the latter part of the day. But I think that by closing places of business at 3 o'clock every employee would be given the opportunity to go out and vote, and I think that would overcome the whole difficulty. The hon. member from South York has suggested voting on Saturday, and the hon. member for London (Mr. Gray) has referred to the convenience of commercial men in relation to voting. We know that in municipal elections in London and in Toronto and some other places arrangements were made whereby the vote was taken on New Year's day, and the experience in our city has shown that there has been a smaller percentage of votes cast at the polls since that innovation. Consequently, voting on the holiday has been of no advantage. As to extending the hours in rural constituencies, I agree with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) that there is no demand from rural constituencies to have extended hours; but I do not think there would be any objection to it if it were found necessary. I would much rather see the same hours exist in rural communities as in cities, so as not to have any discrimination between them. Then how are we to determine what is strictly a rural municipality? My own is a rural constituency, but I have 8,000 people from the city of London who live in the township in my constituency, mechanics and employees in the different shops and factories of London. If that were considered a rural constituency and the hours limited, the workingmen who live there would not have the same opportunity of exercising the franchise as men who live in the city. I think it would be very objectionable and I would resent it if any difference were to be made between the hours of voting as between rural and civic municipalities. I think the difficulty would be overcome if a quarter holiday or half holiday were declared and it were made a sacred duty for every man to exercise his franchise on election day.

I would suggest
that the chairman read clause 5 so that both clauses may be before the committee.
Section 5 read:
The following section is inserted immediately after section 136:
"136a. Every employer shall on polling day give to every voter in his employ one additional hour for voting other than the noon hour, and shall make no deduction in the pay

of such employees nor impose or exact any penalty from any employee by reason of absence during such hour.
In connection with section 5, is there any penalty?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is no special penalty provided by this Bill. There is, as I have no doubt the hon. member is aware, a penalty provided under a general disposition for a violation of the obligations imposed under any statutes for which no particular penalty is prescribed; and I suppose that the enforcement of this, unless we inserted a special penalty, would have to depend on that clause.

Would it not be clearer it there were a penalty attached to that section. I am in favour of section 4 if no better scheme can be devised. I am in favour of giving everybody a chance to vote. I understand that in the cities the labouring classes cannot conveniently vote between the hours of 9 and 5. I would even like to see an hour earlier in the morning if that were possible, but if not I would favour the hours from 9 to 6. I would very much prefer the idea given out by the last speaker of having voting day declared a half holiday. That would serve every constituency, and in default of voting day being declared a half holiday, I would prefer to have section 5 read that instead of one hour every employer shall on voting day give every voter in his employ at least two additional hours. In some cities we know that the factories have many employees voting at one poll and that it would be practically impossible for them all to vote at the one hour.

The suggestion made by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) to extend the hour by commencing at 8 o'clock in the morning would to my mind be the most objectionable one of all, so far as the rural constituencies of the West are concerned. It must be borne in mind that in the western provinces, during the winter months, at 8 o'clock in the morning the sun is just rising, and in stormy weather it would be dark in many parts of the West at that hour. Then very often the officers of the polling division, the deputy returning officer, the poll clerk and the scrutineers of the various candidates, may have to travel 7 or 8 or 10 miles from their homes to reach the polling booth, and therefore it would be a very great hardship to compel them to open the poll at 8 o'clock in the morning. The present hour, so far as rural constituencies are concerned, is very satisfactory; there is no demand from any part of the country for a change, and a change would be resented.
I think that my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Maedonell) has made out a very good case on behalf of the cities. The suggestion of the hon. member for Middlesex (Mr. Ross), that there should be a quarter or a half holiday, seems to me the most reasonable one, although I am not prepared to say just which would work out best. Election day comes on an average only once in four years, and it would be no great hardship if workingmen were allowed to go to work at ten in the morning, or to quit at three in the afternoon. It seems to me that as the polls usually cover only about 200 voters, you would in that way get over the difficulty with as little inconvenience as possible. It will be admitted, after the 'discussion we have had for the last half hour, that there are a great many difficulties in the way, and that it is not easy to makq a law that will be absolutely satisfactory. But I think we should leave the rural constituencies alone. Personally, I am in favour of giving the workmen a quarter day's holiday, rather than of extending the time of polling by one hour. I think the holiday would overcome the difficulty with as little friction as possible.

This was a very live issue in Montreal two years ago. It was taken up by all the labour bodies of the city, and discussed by the city council for several weeks, and finally taken up by the Quebec Legislature, which enacted that during a municipal election in the city of Montreal the polls should open at nine in the morning and remain open until eight in the evening. I think that has given general satisfaction in the city of Montreal.

Representing as I do a rural constituency, with seven townships and ten towns, I feel I shall be carrying out the wishes of my constituents in supporting this proposition. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) is opposed to the polls opening at eight in the morning, and there may be something in his objection, but certainly no good reason has been given to-night why the polls should not be kept open until six o'clock. It is ' true that in in the	rural districts the vote is
largely polled by five o'clock or before, but what serious objection can be made

to the suggestion that the deputy returning officer and the clerks should remain at the booths for an extra hour, in order to give workmen and railway men in large cities an opportunity of polling their votes? And it is not only in the large cities that men are not able to poll their votes. Cities like Chatham, or Sarnia, or Windsor, which have a large number of men at work on the railways or in the shops, would be very glad to have this law enacted, so that the men might have an opportunity of polling their votes up to six o'clock at night. 1 sincerely hope that clauses 4 and 5 will receive the unanimous support of the House.

I do not understand how the suggestion of the hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), that the-polls be kept open until six o'clock, will enable railway men employed on trains to poll their votes. The trains do not necessarily arrive at divisional points at, six o'clock; very often not until midnight. The express trains and the freight trains, particularly arrive at the different stations at different hours, according to the schedule on which they run.

This would
give them an extra hour.

But that extra hour does not necessarily give them an opportunity to vote, because if the trains do not arrive until seven the train hands will have no more opportunity of voting than at present. With regard to the suggestion that a halfholiday be proclaimed on election day, I think it would lead to congesting the voters in the later-houi's of the afternoon, and this congestion would make it more difficult for them to poll their votes during the afternoon than if they had the whole day in which to vote. It does appear to me that if there is to be a holiday declared on election day, it should be the whole day. Or the holiday should be given in the forenoon, so that the men could record their votes in the morning. There is always a certain number of electors who will not poll their votes in the morning. They prefer to come to the poll in the afternoon, and then they remain at the booth and get the results before they leave for home. If in addition to these men who naturally postpone their vote until the afternoon, we are to have all the labouring-men who are employed in the district where the votes are to be recorded, we shall have a congestion of votes

in the afternoon, which will render it quite impossible for them all to record their votes, even before six o'clock. It is quite true that some voters are debarred from the opportunity of voting by reason of the fact that the polls close at five o'clock in the afternoon. Still, I am quite aware of the fact that if the polls remained open until midnight, there would he stili some two or three or more voters who would be late in recording their votes. When they have all day to record them they take their time about it, and I do know that in rural polling subdivisions where there is only a small number of votes to be recorded, there are always two or three or more men who come just in time to see the key turned in the lock, and themselves prevented from entering to record their votes.
The committee which had charge of the revision of the Elections Act entered upon their duties with a desire to remove, as far as possible, all the difficulties tiiat stand in the way of a voter recording his vote. In addition to those classes which have been mentioned this evening, there is another class pf voters who very frequently are unable to record their votes. But the difficulty which prevents them cannot be met by any legislation that I can conceive of. I refer to the large number of deep-sea fishermen who are engaged in the prosecution of the deep-sea fisheries in Nova Scotia. There are in the county of Lunenburg, I am sure, a thousand voters who are employed in the deep-sea fisheries fleet every year, and when an election takes place at any time between the first of May and the first of November these men have not the privilege of recording their votes. They are an intelligent portion of the voting community .in the province of Nova Scotia, and we should all like to see them exercising tne franchise with the same regularity as the electors who are otherwise employed. I would not venture to suggest that this committee could think out any feasible scheme by which these men could be permitted to record their votes, unless there was some sort of a roving commission appointed, to go out with ballot boxes to the fishermen so that they could record their votes. But in view of a suggestion in another direction, which we have had from the committee, and which we shall be called upon to deal with before very long, I am still hopeful that perhaps we can arrive at some means by which the fishermen engaged in the deep-sea fisheries may also have an opportunity of Recording their votes:

As long as I have had
the opportunity of looking into the various kinds of legislation regarding voting that have been proposed either in this House or in other legislatures, it has appeared to me that very many suggestions have come forward, but that after all you cannot get very much better results than you have under the present Act. Somebody is always bringing forward some new suggestion, like those contained in the present Bill. In regard to this section 4, which says that " the polls shall be opened at the hour of eight of the clock in the forenoon and kept open until six of the clock in the afternoon," I say that, so far as rural districts are concerned, there is absolutely no sense or reason for that amendment and that in so far as urban municipalities are concerned, there is still less sense.
Read section 4 in conjunction with section 5, which says that at least one additional hour for voting, other than the noon hour, shall be given by each employer without any deduction from the employee's wages. If you legislate that there shall be a 'halfholiday, that if and so shall be done in order to facilitate, and give longer hours for, voting, it simply means, when you get down to the last analysis, that you have less organization for polling your vote, and you do not do any better than if you had the shorter time.
That is from the politician's standpoint, not from the public standpoint.
That is absolutely from the commonsense standpoint, and my hon. friend ought to know that. I think I have been in politics as long as he has and know as much about them.
I am paying a tribute to the hon. gentleman's knowledge of politics.

I was trying to pay a tribute to my hon. friend's commonsense. If you have a half-holiday, what do you find?-men knocked out of work, congestion of voters during the last hour, or half-hour, at the polls, and the very thing that you have tried to guard against you are up against in a worse form than before. To the two hours to be given to employees on voting day I have no objection. If you give employees in the larger cities from 12 to 2, those who work ir wards a considerable distance from their own polling subdivisions will have a chance to go to the polls and 121
vote. It is easier to get there in two hours than in one hour. If you extend the hours of voting you simply reach the result that, while more time is given to bring in the vote, less organization takes place, everybody puts off what might be done that minute, votes will be polled during the last hour, or at the last minute, and you will be as far short as you were before. In the rural municipalities there is no call whatever for an extension of the voting hours. In urban municipalities I doubt very much if there is any demand for such an amendment to the law, and I believe that we can get along just as well in the future as we have in the past, and that the time between the 'hours of nine and five is quite sufficient to poll the votes, provided you have the necessary organization. You would be no better off with the extra hours and with the extra hours you simply have less organization to get the vote to the polls, and there would be as many votes polled at the last minute as there are now. For these reasons, it does appear to me that although this committee has considered this Bill, and I have no doubt considered it very carefully, we might very well leave the hours of voting as they are to-day, but if the House, or the committee sees fit we might set apart the hours from 12 to 2 for voting. Outside of that we had better leave the whole Act as it is, and not bring in these amendments.

I do not understand the Act to mean what my hon. friend (Mr. Pardee) has stated in so far as it requires the employer to give the employee an opportunity to vote. The Bill says:
Every employer shall on polling day give to every voter In his employ at least one additional hour for voting other than the noon hour, and shall make no deduction in the pay of such employees, nor impose or exact any penalty from any employee by reason of absence during such hour.
I do not understand this, to mean that the employee shall be free from one to two o'clock.	I do not think that would
be a very good thing. It means that the employer shall give to the employees some time during polling hours an extra hour to go to the polls. It does not mean that the employees shall have the right to the hour between one and two o'clock. We would have the same difficulty from congestion at the polls between one and two o'clock if that were the meaning of the section and that would not be in the public interest nor would it assist in polling the votes.	.
It means any time of the day?	.
Yes.
I think that the hour between five and six o'clock would be a very convenient time for the working man.
There is no fixed hour whatever; it means whatever hour will suit them.

-1 come from a constituency which is partly rural and partly urban. Personally, and speaking from observation, I think that the hours from nine to five o'clock are very reasonable hours and that they are all right. I think a half holiday would be an improvement where labour is employed. It would be well for the men to be set free from all influences of the employer for at least half a day. In some places the men are let out perhaps in ones and twos and they go to the poll under very peculiar influences. It would be well if they were given a half holiday and allowed to do as they pleased. With regard to the day of the election, it has been the custom for some time past to hold municipal elections on Monday and I think that is a very good day. It would be a good day for Dominion elections also. Commercial travellers are at home over Sunday as a rule and they could remain at home and poll their votes on Monday before leaving. I think that every .man in this country who has a vote ought to be obliged to poll that vote. It would get rid of a great deal of difficulty in the matter of canvassing and that kind of work. I therefore would approve of a half holiday on the afternoon of election day and I would suggest that the hours continue to be from nine o'clock to five o'clock which I think are very reasonable and give a long enough time for the purpose of polling the vote. If the Government saw fit it would be well to have Monday set apart as election day.

Every hon. gentleman who has risen to oppose this measure admitted before he sat down that it was right in principle. I do not think there is any hon. gentleman who has opposed this Bill who has not at some stage of the discussion suggested something in the way of greater latitude in voting. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Ball) goes farther than any of those who spoke before him. He says	that he is in favour of a
half holiday and of compulsory voting. I commend the hon. gentleman' for that

opinion. It is my opinion. I have introduced compulsory voting legislation into the House in other days for the sole reason that it would practically obliterate ninety-nine per cent of electoral corruption. If men have to go to the poll they will go and vote without being carried there, or without being paid to go there, and they will not remain away because they are paid to remain away. Nothing would purify the election atmosphere so much as compulsory voting, but I realize that is not a proposal which will find acceptance in this country at the present time. Every hon. gentleman who has opposed this Bill has said something in its favour. I commend the opinion of my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin). I think he is quite right in more senses than one. The hon. gentleman, without mentioning it, quoted the Ontario law which gives two hours during election day to enable employees to vote. He also commended the idea of giving a portion of the day as a holiday. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) did not seem to see any reason for this legislation. It is suggested that .he cannot see anything, but sometimes he is pretty wide awake. I w.ant to tell the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who is a very reasonable gentleman, that in the city of Toronto, notwithstanding what my hon. friend would call the herculean efforts of the great Tory party in that city, and notwithstanding the efforts made by both parties, we poll on an average of only from 60 to 65 per cent of the total vote. There are about 50,000 or 60,000 voters in that city. In the last election in the riding of South Toronto, which I have the honour to represent, the vote polled was only a little over 60 per cent of the total vote.
You had enough?
I had enough for the occasion.
If you had needed the rest, you would have had it polled.

You never can tell, until after an election is over, how you stand. Very much the greater portion of that 40 per cent of the vote that is not polled is not polled because there are no sufficient opportunities or facilities given to the people to poll their votes. In the district of Toronto referred to, part of which is represented by my hon. friend the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean), there is a population of three-quarters of

a million people, and it is impossible for them, residing as they do at very great distances from their work, to poll their votes during business hours. The section that follows is not sufficient to afford relief, because the one hour that is given is not enough. The experience of the Ontario Government has been that at least two hours are needed in cities to give men an opportunity to get back to their residential districts for the pnrpose of voting. The legislation has been progressive there; and as pointed out by my hon. friend the member for East 'Toronto (Mr. Kemp), the Ontario Government has recently enacted that, in cities of 200,000, the polls shall open at eight o'clock in the morning. Who is hurt in a city, if the polls are opened at eight o'clock in the morning and kept open until six o'clock -at night? Even in the country, people would not be hurt.
What are the hours for polling in municipal elections in Toronto?

They were changed
recently. I understand the polls are open until six o'clock now.
In Montreal they are kept open until eight o'clock.

And that is not too
long to keep them open. If men get an [DOT]opportunity to vote, they will vote, and the expense of taking them to the polls will not be necessary. I appeal to the committee to make reasonable and fair provision for people in the city districts, who number now quite forty per cent of the total population of the Dominion. If section 4 is allowed to pass with a proper amendment so as to exclude the country districts, the committee will be doing justice to all parties.
Section negatived.

I beg to move the following amendment to section 4:
Provided that in cities having a population of over 200,000, and in ridings formed in part by a portion or portions of such cities, the polls shall be opened in every polling place at eight o'clock in the forenoon and shall be kept open until five o'clock in the afternoon of the same day and the vote shall be by ballot.
This amendment amounts to practically nothing, and I hope it will be adopted unanimously by the committee. It is simply the Ontario law applied to cities of 200,000 people and upwards. It applies to only two or three cities in Canada, which are very congested districts. Relief will be given, and the ipoll-s will close uniformly 1214
throughout Canada at five o'clock in the afternoon.

The time is not the same throughout Canada and the results are known in Halifax while voting is going on in the West. It is no relief to the city people to open the polls earlier in the morning. If you want to give them relief, you will have to keep the polls open until later in the .evening. That is the mature judgment of the Montreal Labour Council and of all the labour organizations of the cities.

Why not say " in the
cities of Canada?"	[DOT]
. Mr. A. K. MACLEAN: If my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) carried that amending clause, a constituency partly rural and partly urban would incur a very serious difficulty. It might happen that 95 per cent of his polling districts within that electoral district would close at five, and the result be known before, say, halfpast five or a quarter to six.

The hon. gentleman
has not grasped the purpose bf the amendment. It is that in all cities, or in ridings that are formed in part by city districts the polls shall open at eight o'clock and close at five o'clock.
That is what I am speaking about. I am pointing out the serious objection that 95 per cent of the polling stations of one electoral district close at five and the other 5 per cent at six.

The same closing
hour applies to any riding that includes in part or whole a city of '200,000 or over.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the first place, this amendment is going to make the law in two cities in Canada different from the law for the rest of the country. That is not an insuperable objection, but it is an undesirable thing unless, by the differentiation, you are going to get a very substantial advantage for some class of the people. Speaking for myself, I have very strong sympathy with what was put forward on behalf of the railway and the workingmen, and I believe that we ought to do what we can to make it possible for both these classes to vote absolutely independently, without any question of asking time and taking time and so forth. While my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell) says that he regretted that the committee were not disposed to take up and work out the proposition of the railway men, I do not think that exactly describes the

action of the committee. The committee were disposed to take the question up, and my memory is that they took it up and that they endeavoured to work it out on a practical basis; but they could not find a method by which the railway men could vote the day previous to election day, which was the suggestion they put forward. It was considered that, failing that, a substantial advantage might come to them by opening the polls at an earlier hour in the morning, and the hour suggested was six o'clock or half-past six o'clock in the morning, so as to enable the men to vote before they went to the stations. This would also have enabled a large number of the labouring classes to vote before they went to their work. The reason given for lengthening the hours does not seem to me the important one. It is not that you want more hours of polling, but you want the polls open at the time when the people are best able to vote. From the point of view of the cities, if you are going to allow the workingman to vote before he goes to work in the morning, you would have to open the polls before seven o clock. I do not see how it is going to help the workingman to open the polls at eight o'clock.
But if he has two hours in the middle of the day, would not that do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That comes under a different section. I was pointing out certain considerations in relation to this particular proposal. I do not know how it is in the rural constituencies, but in Montreal the workingman goes to work at seven o'clock. By opening the poll at eight you might help the clerks and others who go to their offices at nine, but the change would not help the workingman. The great difficulty in the cities is that if a man does not vote before he goes to his business, or finds the poll closed when he returns from his business, he must make a special trip over a long distance from his place of occupation to the place where he polls his vote in the subdivision in which he resides. It will be a great benefit, it seems to me, to provide. a time, what we may call a free time, for the voter when he can poll his vote, and thus obviate the necessity of conveying him to the poll.
It is only once in four years he is called upon to vote and he is not very seriously inconvenienced.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know; but what I am pointing out is that the section as proposed
fMr. Doherty.]
does not fulfil the purpose for which it is intended so far as the cities are concerned.
It is for you to assume the responsibility of doing that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is for the House; I cannot impose my power upon the House; it is essentially a matter for Parliament to pronounce upon. I do not think it would be fair for me, even if I could, to impose my will upon the members of the House.
The effect of the suggested amendment of the hon. member for South Toronto is to make a different law for these two cities out of the whole Dominion. It
10 p.m. does not seem to me to gain the advantage which we wish to gain. My own constituency is substantially a workingman's constituency, and I have a large railway men's vote. It will not help these voters to give them an hour extra in the morning by making the polls open at eight o'clock. The workingman is at work before eight o'clock, and he will not gain by the extension of an hour. No doubt it would be of some advantage to the class of people who go to their offices at nine, but I do not see that that advantage is sufficient to make it worth while to differentiate between these cities and the rest of the country.
The minister criticises my amendment because it does not put the hour's increase of time at the end of the day. That motion was before the Chair and did not receive support.

I am more or less sympathetic with the desire of the hon. member for South Toronto. I do not think that anybody, on the abstract question of whether the polls shall open at seven or eight in the morning and continue open until six in the evening, could make a successful argument against it. It is not an argument against the polls being open from seven o'clock a.m. until six o'clock p.m. that all the votes are polled by five o'clock. On the other hand, I admit there is no apparent necessity for this change, so far as the rural districts are concerned. I am inclined to agree with the Minister of Justice in regard to the amendment of the hon. member for South Toronto; it will accomplish very little if anything to open the polls at eight in the morning. If it were six o'clock-	_
I will change it to six if the hon. member will support it.

I have not suggested that. As the amendment would

appear to accomplish so little, I think we might as well have the section as it is at . present.
Amendment (Mr. Macdonell) negatived.

That section 5 be amended by substituting Hie words " two hours " for " hour."
He said: I am open for any suggestion so long as the facilities for voting are increased, and they have not been increased so far. I desire to call attention to the Ontario Act. This is chapter 8 of the Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1914, section 112. It is well worded and has worked out well:
A voter entitled to vote within a city or town shall, on the day of polling be entitled to absent himself for the purpose of voting from any service or employment in which he is then engaged or employed, from the hour of noon until the hour of two of the clock next thereafter, and a voter shall not, because of his so absenting himself, be liable to any penalty, or suffer or incur any reduction from the wages or compensation to which but for his absence he would have been entitled, but this section shall not apply where a voter is by his employer permitted or allowed at any other period during the hours of polling, reasonable and sufficient time and opportunity to vote.
This is an exceedingly fair and just provision.
In what year was that introduced?

Seven or eight years ago. It amply protects the voter against unfair discrimination on the part of the employer, and it does not apply if the employer gives the employee ample time at any other time to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that not the substance of the provision contained in this proposed legislation? We give the employee an hour in addition to the noon hour.

Nowadays, as the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) remarked, workmen work an hour more each day in order to get a halfholiday on Saturday, and the consequence is that in many cases they do not get an hour for lunch at noon. The Ontario legislation gives the employee two definite hours; I commend the language of this section to the consideration of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Ontario legislation gives two definite hours, but only if the employer does not give his employee sufficient time at some other hour of the day. We say simply that the employer shall give these two hours. Suppose I am an employer, and
I say to my employee you cannot get from 12 until 2 o'clock, but I will give you an hour at another time, then, if that is a sufficiently long time for him to go to vote, I shall be perfectly right, under the Ontario statute, and no complaint can be made. We are saying in effect, but in shorter form, the same thing, because we say: you shall give the employee an hour besides the noon hour. If the employee does not take the noon hour, that is his own affair. In drawing this provision we had the Ontario section before us, and we thought we had adopted the Ontario section, but in simpler form.
Only as to one hour.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: When you say one hour in addition to the noon hour, that is two. hours.
That is not what the Bill says.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It says that the employer shall give to every voter in his employ at least one additional hour for voting, other than the noon hour. If any other words will make the meaning clearer, I shall be glad to adopt them. If the employee chooses to agree with his employer that he shall not take the noon hour, I do not see that we should' be called upon to say that he shall get some other hour than that. He makes his own bargain with his employer about the noon hour. Really I think there may be a question as to the desirability of fixing specific hours, but I only want to point out that the Ontario legislation does not do that any more than this does.

The object of this legislation is to provide that the voter shall have a chance to vote. I take it that everybody wants to make it just as easy for the voter to vote as it is possible to make it. Taking into consideration the fact that you must have in the first place, the voter's interest, and that it is desired to give the employee a chance to vote, irrespective of what his employer may think, would it not be well to provide that the hours during which the employee may vote on election day shall be from twelve o'clock noon until two p.m.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That might create a
situation in which many industries would have to close during the remainder of the day, because all employees would go out at the same time.
Will this hour be chosen by the employer, or by the employee?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The obligation of the
employer is to give the employee an hour other than the noon hour, and it would seem to be a fair thing that the employer should fix the hour that is most suitable. At all events, that is the effect of the section.

My apprehension
was that the hour that is mentioned here as the noon hour is referred to only inferentially; the provision is not as clear as the provision of the Ontario Act. The difficulty, which is rather more deep-seated than has been suggested by the minister, is that while the Ontario Act makes provision for a man's having two hours of his employer's time once in every three, four or five years, the hour spoken of in this Bill at the noon hour is a period of time contributed by the employee himself.
That is he is out a part of it; he is paid by the hour usually and he is out the time he is not working; so that all he gets, so far as . he gets anything gratis under this Bill, is one hour given to him in addition to his noon hour.

Would that not be fair
after all?

I think all he gets
by this Bill is the one hour. That seems to be the intention of the committee and of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One hour besides the
noon hour.
We could not hold up our trains for an hour; in the case of any employees not operating trains there would be no objection.

I save that by the
proposal here. The law now applies to the company railways and I propose to apply it to the Intercolonial or Government Railway system with the saving clause that it shall not apply to those the performance

of whose duties is necessary to the operation Of the regular trains.

Have you a similar
clause with reierence to the other railways? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As our section reads
without any exception at all, applying to every employer and employee, I suppose it would so operate that the railways would have to stop their trains and let the men go out and vote and that certainly ought to be provided against.
Inasmuch as no special hour is fixed at which the company railways are to accord an hour to the employees for voting I uo not think the amendment is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I understand the difficulty to be met is that a railway conductor who goes out on a train at 8 o'clock would be a great many miles away in a very short time.

Has there been any
difficulty in the past on account of Government railways in this respect?

It is proposing an
amendment which applies to all railways, and I understand that the minister accepts the proposition, as one that should apply to the Government railways as to the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We might insert this
addition:
This section shall apply to railway companies and to Government railways and their employees with the exception of employees engaged in the running of trains and to whom such time could not be given without interfering with the running of the trains.
What would be the effect of that amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the first place to
