make it applicable to Government railways and in the second place to make it clear that with regard to all railways they would not be under obligation to give an hour to men engaged in the running of trains, to whom they could not give an hour without stopping the trains.
Could not the minister go a little further and say the running of regular trains?

The runmg of a special
train might be of much more importance than the running of a regular train.

Would the minister's
amendment apply to street railways? Because if all men on street railways were entitled to a couple of hours it might disorganize transportation in cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman think it would? As they would not all have to be given their hour off at the same time it would surely be possible to arrange the schedule so as not to interfere with the working of the system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I presume that street railway employees, like others, have a dinner hour. We aire not making them give two hours. I assume that these employees already have an hour for their dinner. Personally, I am not in a position to say how it will affect the running of a street railway system in a large city.
Do I understand that the minister moves that amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: To be absolutely frank, I am not perfectly satisfied with it, because when one comes to look at it, we have other systems of transportation besides railways. During the period of summer navigation there may be many voters employed on steamboats.
You could not make it apply to vessels unless they were in port.

Has there been any
request for this legislation? I have not heard of a case where an employer refused to let an employee go out and vote, whether he was on the opposite side of politics or not. It seems to me we are passing legislation that has not been asked for, and that there is no public demand or necessity for. It is imposing an obligation which is not at all necessary.

I am sorry the hon. gentleman was not in the House when we were considering it. A section has been passed as part of the Dominion Elections Act that employers shall on polling day give to the voters in their employ at least one additional hour beyond the noon hour for voting purposes. That was passed some time ago, and the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) was simply moving an amendment that it should apply to employees on the Intercolonial who would be exempt from the provision of that section
unless it were specifically stated otherwise by Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: So far as the demand for it is concerned, we have had very numerous and clearly representative delegations from workmen's organizations asking that we should give a whole day or a half-day's holiday in order that the men might vote. Since I have had the honour of being in the House I know that the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) has on several occasions proposed a measure to that end, and I think a great many of us have received very strong representations on the subject from representatives of organized workmen in the big cities. So whether the demand ought to be met or not, I do not think it can 'be said that this legislation was not asked for.

It is imposing a fine on an employer of labour. If a man employs 200 men and lets them off for an hour, he will lose 200 hours' work. If he had 500 men, he would lose 500 hours' work. This will make election day an expense to every employer of labour in Canada, and it does not seem to me to be right.

Before this Bill is finally disposed of I should like to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to some very desirable amendments to chapter 26 of the Revised Statutes of 1908. This chapter provides for the preparation of voters' lists in those portions of Ontario that are not under municipal organization. At the time it was passed it was no doubt veTy carefully thought out, but in practice it does not work out as well as it .should. For instance, these lists have always been revised after the proclamation for an election, or within the last thirty or forty days before polling day. During that time the judges have to select the polling subdivisions, and the voter must necessarily be an actual resident within the polling subdivision for which the revision is being made. In other words, a man who has 'been residing in an unorganized township takes a few steps across the road into an organized township, and he is absolutely debarred from voting. Simply because he was not an actual resident of the unorganized territory he is not allowed to vote in the organized territory. Since the passing of this Act two thousand voters in my district have been deprived of the privilege of voting. The Act is also very cumbersome. For instance, why should it be necessary to have in an

unorganized district a board of three judges to consider appeals that might be made against the voters' lists, when in a large township with five or ten times the population the work is done by one county judge. Surely if one county judge is able to do this work in the larger cities he ought to be able to do it in districts where the population is sparse. I am calling these matters to the attention of the minister because they are somewhat important to me. I have forty polls of this nature with probably a voting population of 5,000. I think this state of affairs should be remedied. If it cannot be done on this particular occasion perhaps before the Bill is finally passed some way can be thought out for giving these men the right to vote. Let me point out further that the Ontario law makes matters a lot worse, because the province has separate voters' lists. These lists are posted up in the post office, and a man may see his name on them and not pay sufficient attention to see that it is only a provincial list, not a Dominion list. Then when the Dominion list is printed by the King's Printer he finds he is not in for that section at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no doubt there is a great deal in what the hon. member says, and no doubt the question is important. But I am afraid that for us to enter upon an examination of the law with regard to the making of lists with a view to remedying it, would be rather difficult at this stage of the session. However, I do not expect the Bill to have its third reading this evening and before it comes to third reading I will look into what has been said, and see if it is possible for us to deal with the situation.
I beg to move that section 5 be amended by adding thereto the following words:
This section shall apply to railway companies and to the Government railways and their employees with the exception of employees engaged in the running of trains and to whom such time cannot he given without interfering with the running of the trains.
What penalty is provided for failure to comply with this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This particular section does not provide a penalty for failure to comply with it. It was thought that it might be left to the application of the general provision which does provide a penality for the violation of a statute where no specific penalty is prescribed.

Section 269 might apply.
tMr. Arthurs.]

In regard to the Government railway proposition, we would not want- to take proceedings against my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Cochrane), because that would be a very drastic procedure and probably he would not know anything about the violation of the Act. If there was some local official who transgressed the law there should be some way by which he could be reached.
I nominate Mr. Gutelius.
I think you had better leave the Act alone unless you know what you are doing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that section 269 would apply, but I am quite satisfied that there is a penalty for the violation of any statutory disposition where no specific penalty is prescribed.
In the Election Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, in the Criminal-Code. I have sent for the statutes to find the clause.

Perhaps we might let that section stand until the minister looks into it and comes to a conclusion in regard to it.
Section allowed to stand.
On section 7-form of nomination paper amended to require address for service of papers:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only change in the nomination paper is that in the new form the candidate is required to insert his address. That is in view of the provision in the Bill to amend the Controverted Elections Act that service in any contestation shall be validly made if addressed to the candidate at the address mentioned in his nomination paper.
That would mean simply his post office address?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, we are suggesting to the House to provide in that Act that mailing to the address would be sufficient
service.
Progress reported.

On motion of Hon. C. J. Doherty, Bill No. 109, to amend the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, was read the second time,

and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Sevigny in the Chair.
On section 1-names of courts:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The purpose of the repealing clauses i and vidi of paragraph J of section 2 of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, chapter 7, Revised Statutes, 1906, is to make the names of the courts mentioned in the Act correspond with their present names. In Ontario the name of the court has been changed and likewise in Saskatchewan and Alberta they now have the Supreme Court of the province. In the Act as it stands the court is referred to in this way:
In the province of Saskatchewan or Alberta, the Supreme Court of the Northwest territories pending the abolition of that court by the legislature of the province, and thereafter such Superior Court of justice as, in respect of the civil jurisdiction of the said court, is established for the province in lieu thereof.
The court now established is the Supreme Court of the province.
What are subsections 3 and 4 of section 2 which are repealed?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Subsection 3 of section 2 of the present Act is as follows:
In respect of proceedings relating to or affecting an election for an electoral district partly in the province of Saskatchewan and partly in the province of Alberta, the court shall he the Supreme Court of the Northwest territories pending the abolition of that court by the legislature of the province of Alberta, and thereafter such Superior Court as, in respect of the civil jurisdiction of that court, is established for that province in lieu thereof.
I understand that there is no constituency now that is partly in each province and there is therefore no need for that provision. Furthermore there is no long-or any Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories. Subsection 4 was a provision to cover a transient condition. It was as follows:
Proceedings under this Act which are pending in the Supreme Court of the Northwest territories in the province of Saskatchewan or the province of Alberta at the time of the abolition of the said court in the province may be continued in such Superior Court of justice, as, in respect of the civil jurisdiction of the said court, is established for the province in lieu thereof in all respects as if such proceedings had been instituted in such latter court.
The section ceases to have any operation.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-proof of right to be a petitioner:
This section is very drastic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is intended to be drastic. In the view of the committee, it was not of material importance who presented the petition. The provisions of the Act with regard to security and so forth were looked upon as a sufficient protection to the party whose election might be attacked. Experience has shown that discussions with regard to the exact proof of the identity of the person who is the petitioner, .and that he is a person whose name is upon the list, have been such a productive field for preliminary objections and discussions of no material bearing upon the substantial question as to whether the respondent was illegally or corruptedly elected, that it .appeared to us that we would be justified in making the proof sufficient that the petitioner's name appears upon the list that is produced. This will apply to the great majority of cases, because in the bulk of cases there are lists. Where there are no lists, or where the petitioner is petitioning in his quality as candidate and his name might not be on the list, it is thought that an affidavit should be sufficient. There is ample protection in the affidavit, in the great facility with which it would lie within the power of the party whose election was attacked, to ascertain and prosecute for perjury, if any one who was not a candidate, swore that he was a candidate.

A man, who nas a minor and who might not be entitled to vote at an election at all, might be a petitioner; simply because his name appears on the voters' list by fraud or inadvertence. You cannot go beyond the list and have the petition presented by a person who has a right to present a petition.
What is the difference?
Why not use any one's name? Why say that the petitioner shall be a voter?
That is quite true, but you must have' designated by the statute some class from which the petitioner can be drawn.	.
If you permit any class to come in, then why make any condition at all?

The electoral lists
practically include every one who is 21 years of age and a British subject within

an electoral division. That is pretty wide, and any one who is on that list can be a petitioner.
He might not be a qualified person, and yet be on the list.
As the law stood before, it was open to the respondent to come into court and say that the petitioner, while his name was on the list, was disqualified as a petitioner. It was very anomalous.
Why?
Because the point really at issue should not be affected one way or the other by who the petitioner is.
Then why have a petitioner at all?
If the hon. gentleman can provide some machinery by which he can try out a petition without a petitioner, all very well.

Who has a right in the ordinary course? There is something due to the candidate as well as to the petitioner. Why should the candidate be harassed by a. man of straw? Why should not the petitioner be responsible for costs?
He gives security of
And the costs may go to

When the hon. member sees the remaining provisions of the Bill, he will see that the trials of election petitions are very much expedited, and that there will be less costs because there will be fewer appeals.
If the remaining provisions are as bad as this, they must be very bad.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-repealing sections 6 and 7:
Is section 2 passed?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes.
I wish to register my objection.

There is a provision in the Dominion Elections Act by which a man whose name may be on the list becomes disqualified by his own act. Perhaps that provision in the law is repealed somewhere here, but there is a section of the law as it stands to-day which says that any man who hires a team to take an elector to the poll is ipso facto disqualified. That man

can not file a petition. There is a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to that effect. Unless that section is repealed, it will be in conflict with this proposed legislation.

This dispenses with the
need of an affidavit on the part of the petitioner?
It dispenses with everything.
The affidavit should remain. If a petitioner alleges charges against a member of this House, he should substantiate them by affidavit.

The petitioner under this proposed legislation might be a minor; he might be an alien enemy; he might not have a vote at all, his name might be on the list by fraud and misrepresentation; yet he could be a petitioner. He might be even in that delectable institution known as the Kingston penitentiary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: He would not have an opportunity to file a petition.
You might let him sign.

I do not wish to oppose any strenuous objection against the work of this committee being approved, but I am inclined to think that unless some serious objection can be pointed out to the present statute it would be better to leave it alone. Practitioners have become familiar with the present statute, and they get along pretty well with it. If we change the law, it will take twenty years to have the courts interpret it and find out what it means. There will be more trouble, more litigation and more delay than will take place if we continue to act under the present law. I would leave the Act just as it is. It seems anomalous to declare that the petition shall be presented by a voter and then provide that even if his affidavit is absolutely false, it shall be conclusive evidence that he is a voter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt about the fact mentioned by the hon. member that the courts have a jurisprudence on the law as it now stands, and that the practitioners have become familiar with it; but what we have become familiar with is the fact that under the law as it now stands, and its practical application under that jurisprudence, and the way in which cases may be conducted, a party petitioned against may

sit through the Parliament to which he was not legally elected.
The purpose of this Bill is to remedy in this instance what seems to us a serious evil. As the law operates it practically comes to this:	that a party who is protested sits through the greater part of a Parliament without any determination being reached as to whether he is lawfully elected or not. Looking at this section alone, it may appear that the Bill takes up a hostile attitude, if I may use that expression, to the party whose election is attacked, but I think that before we get through the Bill it will be seen that there are provisions that operate also to protect the party rightfully fighting a contestation.
Why not let this clausestand?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection, if
hon. gentlemen wish time to consider the provisions of the Bill, to let the whole Bill stand. I may point out that the committee gave a good deal of time to this measure and it seemed to us that it was a desirable measure. Of course, if the House thinks it is not a matter of sufficient importance to call for the attention at this stage of the session, or if the House thinks that it is so important that further time is necessary, I have no objection to allow it to stand.

I would suggest that
tne committee go through the Bill now, allowing controversial sections to stand. Surely, there are some sections that would meet with the general approval and in going through the Bill we will get a better understanding of the whole measure. To meet my view the Bill would have to be considerably modified. I do not think we should encourage petitions, because usually the sitting member obtains his election in the proper manner.
Oh, oh.

I am surprised at the
ribald laughter of some hon. members. They evidently think otherwise.

The matter of
improving the Controverted Elections Act has been under discussion in this House for a great number of years, and I am surprised to hear the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Pugsley) say that nothing should be done. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has given the subject consideration or not, but unless he has I think he should not make a suggestion
that the Bill should not be considered. It is not a very lengthy measure, and will not take very much time to consider. As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has pointed out, the fact is the Controverted Elections Act is a nullity, and
11 p.m. every member of Parliament should consider himself bound in duty to make that Act a living force.
I do not like to hear any hon. member suggest that we should abandon the whole Bill. I would rather entertain the suggestion that we should repeal the whole Controverted Elections Act.
Is it not attempted by this Bill to make the Controverted Elections Act a living farce instead of a living force?
I fancy the hon. gentleman has not read the Bill and cannot tell-
I have read one section, and that is sufficient.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman's reading and understanding of the Bill is not quite complete; perhaps the measure would stand a little further consideration on his part. I do not think there is anything unfair in section 2. The whole purpose of the Bill is to expedite the trial of election petitions. It eliminates preliminary objections and it provides a simpler method for the service of petitions and any process under the Act, and I think that is, in the main, a just provision.
How does this clause carry out, or assist to carry out, the proposal the hon. gentleman has spoken of?

The hon. gentleman
knows, I suppose, that a great difficulty of petitioners under the Controverted Elections Act is in effecting service. Respondents leave the country, and when service has been attempted to be made in foreign countries the courts have held it back. Why should not service of the petition be made-
That has nothing to do with section 2.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We are on section 3.

I do not know that
I can say anything .further than has been said by the Minister of Justice. Anybody whose name is on an election petition is presumed to be a voter having the right to petition against the person elected. I think that should be prima facie evidence of his ability to petition.

Does not that make it
possible for irresponsible parties through a solicitor to file petitions merely to cause annoyance to a person elected?
No more so than to-day -there is no more opportunity for irresponsible persons to be petitioners than today.

I was on the
committee that considered this Bill. I was not on it originally, but took the place of the former member from Prince Albert, Judge Mackay. I am free to say that these other gentlemen would not say, that the chairman of the committee, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) gave this matter much more attention than is usually given by committees to the matters referred to them. The sole desire of the committee was to find an expeditious and efficient method whereby elections that had been fraudulently contested should be .set aside and those responsible for the wrong-doing in those elections quickly brought to justice. It may be that the legislation is disputatious in the broad sense of the term, but in a still broader sense it is legislation that, if placed upon the statute book, will help to improve public life and possibly do away with some of the stories we read from time to time in the press-not confined to one party but the common heritage of both-with relation to elections. If we can legislate to improve the conditions of public life, to make it possible for elections to be run without having recourse to money and to corrupt practices which are too often had recourse to in Canada, it would be a good thing. Of course, this cannot be done in a day. Walpole, in his time, declared that every man had his price. It took a long time to bring about the conditions that exist in England to-day. I think too much can not be said for the work given to this measure by the chairman of this committee .and the junior member for Halifax-to single these gentlemen out among those who were deserving. I think this should be treated as a serious matter by this House. If we can do something to make it a little harder to get away with corruption and corrupt influences and the destroying of the body politic, I think we shall have done a good thing.

It was thought by every member of the committee that the law in respect of election protests as it now stands 
is practically a nullity; the only purpose which it serves is that of a club, to be wielded by a political opponent in order to protect himself or to arrange a saw-off. I take it that the hon. member for Kings and Albert does not take kindly to the provisions of this Bill. If the hon. gentleman accepts the principle that a simpler and more concise method of getting after corruption in elections is necessary, then this Bill will commend itself to his judgment. If, on the other hand, he takes the ground that the law is all right as it is, the provisions of the Bill will not appeal to him. It is provided, in the first place, that any person may file a petition so long as he puts up $1,000. The real fact of the matter is that the $1,000, not the personal standing of the petitioner, is the protection to the respondent. The meanest subject of the realm has the right to lay information in the courts of the country if he thinks a crime has been committed. If it is the honest intention of Parliament to provide machinery by which corruption at elections may be put down-my hon. friend and myself could, perhaps, give a good deal of information on this subject.
Speak for yourself.

I speak for my hon. friend as well. If any person has the right to lay an information in a court of law, then any person has the right to sign an election petition, provided his name is on the voters' list and he complies with the requirements of the law. I would have gone further and reduced the deposit to $500, but it was thought best to leave it as it is. We all know, too, that one of the great bones of contention in the past has been the matter of the service of election petitions. Let me give the hon. member for Kings and Albert an illustration, one with which he is probably familiar. The law of New Brunswick provides that the service of the writ must be made in a certain way; that it must be published in a newspaper, served on the respondent and posted in the registry office. The officer to whom the paper was given posted it on a bill-board in the lobby of the court house; the registry office was in the court house. I was counsel for the respondent in that case, and I contended that the publication had not been carried out according to law. I took the ground that posting the notice on a bill-board in the lobby of the court house was not posting it in the registry office. It may surprise my hon. friend to know that the Supreme Court of New Brunswick held that I was right.

It does not surprise me
at all

This kind of thing has a tendency not to facilitate the trial of election petitions, but to put all kinds of technical objections in the way. The question resolves itself into a consideration of whether we shall have election petitions, or whether we shall not have them. If we are to have them, then it is well to provide simply that a copy of the petition shall be mailed to the address given in the nomination paper.

I am not finding fault
with that, I am in favour of that.
I am glad we have converted my hon. friend to that extent.

The hon. member for
Carleton evidently thinks that he is the only person who desires fairness and purity in elections. I am just as anxious as he is that a man should be properly elected, and that if he is not properly elected he should be punished by the loss of his seat. But I want the Act to be a proper one. I believe in fair-play and protection, both for the man who is elected and for the man who is defeated. One would almost think, from the remarks of the hon. gentleman, that a man has committed a crime because he is elected; that because he happens to be elected, it is his duty to be unseated. I do not look at it that way at all. The man who is elected has a right to the protection of the law; yet everything is done to harass him. Even an alien, it is contended, should have the right to file a petition against him. Let the service be as simple as. possible; send the paper, if you will, to his known place of residence. 1 care not how simple you make the service, but I do say that you should provide that the man who files the petition shall be a duly qualified voter. Why should he not be a duly qualified voter? What right has he to object if he is not? [DOT]
Did the hon. gentleman not say a few moments ago -that he would have no objection to the ordinary process of issuing a writ?
Yes.
What about the alien who puts up security?

The point is that he does not put up sufficient security. If he should put up a bond for the costs, then it would be all right; I would not care who filed the petition. I am sure that
every member of this committee 'is just as desirous as the hon. member for Carle-ton is that elections shall be properly conducted. The hon. gentleman has said that he knows a great deal about corruption; perhaps in his zeal to be elected he did transgress, but I do not propose that he shall plead guilty for me to that charge. I am always very careful to amid even the appearance of evil, so anxious am I not to do anything wrong in connection with elections. I do not see why it should not be required that the person who files a petition shall be a legally qualified voter. All he has to do is to prove that he is on the voters' list; that he has the necessary qualifications, that he is a British subject-surely he can prove these things easily enough. Where is there a chance for any preliminary objection in connection with that, if he is Teally a duly qualified voter, if he has the qualifications and is a British subject?
There have been very serious contests as to the qualification of the petitioner.

Because the conditions have not been fulfilled. My hon. friend speaks of the case in Carleton county. I do not know why he drags that case in because it has nothing to do with the matter under discussion. The Supreme Court of New Brunswick was absolutely right, in my opinion, in holding that the lobby of the court house was not within the registry office. I do not see how they could have held anything else; I think that is good law. Therefore it has nothing to do with this matter. By changing the Act as is proposed you are not going to avoid questions of that kind occurring; if you do not follow the conditions here, your petition will be set aside. There are certain conditions to be observed and if you do not observe them your petition will be set aside as in the other case. Perhaps you are making the conditions less onerous, but why can you not make this law simple in its action and yet require that a man filing a petition shall have some status in the community, that he shall be a legally qualified voter. That is all I ask.
That is hard to determine at times.
I do not think it is hard to determine. It depends simply on his being a British subject, on his having the residence, being of the proper age and being on the voters' list.
That would not prove him a legally qualified voter.
Suppose he is disqualified.
But the burden of proof is on the other side to show that he is disqualified. If he has these qualifications he is a qualified voter legally, prima facie.

Does not my hon. friend see he is getting back to the very condition of affairs that we are trying to eliminate, to the preliminary objections. I know enough about elections to be aware that one of the principal causes of objection is the question of the qualification of the petitioner. In very many election trials the petitioner has been brought up and examined from time to time prior to the trial and the question arises has he been disqualified by bribery, has he committed a corrupt act? If so he would not be qualified. Many petitions have been knocked out on that very matter; you raise a preliminary objection and get into the Supreme Court of Canada and lose a year or two of time. I ask the hon. member if he is not arguing for the continuing of the system of preliminary objections.

Does my hon. friend
think that a man who has violated the election law and disqualified himself is the person to go into court? He should be like the complainant in any other case, the man who goes into court should have clean hands. But he goes in a disqualified person. I do not think that a man who is disqualified should be permitted to file a petition, and the onus of proof of the disqualification is on the respondent because if the petitioner shows he has fulfilled the conditions, that is all he has to show, and it is up to the other side to prove that he is disqualified.

But he is petitioning
not on account of himself alone, but of a large element of the public.

But the man who petitions on behalf of a large element of the public must have a right to do so and that right lies in his being a qualified voter; he represents the qualified electors. They are the only ones who Can say who should be elected. Does he not belong to that class? There are very few constituencies with less than 4,000 or 5,000 qualified voters, and surely within the half or one-third of that number who support the minority candidate there must be enough duly qualified electors to file the petition. If there are not 
the petition had better go unfiled. It seems to me that from every standpoint we should require that the man should be a qualified voter. Simplify procedure as much as you like, but let the individuals who are parties to the trial-because, after all, the petitioner is the party, although he represents a considerable portion of the electorate-let these be the proper persons and then simplify your procedure as much as you like, and I am with you, but I am not with you to permit any sort of straw-man to be put up for the purpose of annoying and putting to trouble a person who has received, according to the electoral returns, the majority of the votes" in any constituency.

I understand that my
hon. friend's principal objection is on the question of the petitioner. When he interrupted some time ago, as he had a right to do, I was pointing out the general purport of the Bill, and I had got over two points. The third principle which we tried to work out in this Bill was that the trial should be brought on almost at once. We all know that under the present law an election trial cannot take place until after all preliminary objections are decided, which sometimes takes two or three years, and it cannot be tried while Parliament is in session. We have tried to eliminate that and bring the practice very nearly to the ordinary practice in a civil suit in court. The petition takes the place of the statement of claim; provision is made that an answer shall be filed, and if it is not filed within fifteen days the clerk of the court files the answer and the petition is immediately at issue and the trial takes place regardless of whether Parliament be in session or not. That practically would be all the principles involved in the Bill that are different from the present law. We have left all the rest of the law as it is, we have left in the provision for preliminary examination of witnesses. We have provided also that a witness can be gathered in very early in the game, in fact you can apply to a judge almost at the time the petition is filed and have an order given that a certain person be examined. That prevents the witnesses getting out of the country.
These are the four cardinal principles involved in the Bill. I am very much in favour of the Bill, although I do not take credit for having originated the idea; I think it came from the Minister of Jus-

tice himself. The minister certainly has done all he could in order to make the Bill perfect. I want to say to the credit of the hon. gentleman (who occupies that position (Mr. Doherty) that I have never in my life seen in a deliberative body a gentleman who has more earnestly tried to work out a perfect scheme which would attain the object in view than has the Minister of Justice in working out this scheme. There has not been a move, there has not been a proposition put forward that appealed to his judicial mind as calculated to work out successfully and prevent bribery and corruption, but the Minister of Justice has adopted it. When it appeared to him, from his long experience as otherwise he was not at all afraid to say so. I do not think there has ever been a committee in the House of Commons that has been as thoroughly in harmony over the principles involved in any measure as this Election Committee in reference to this Bill.
To go back to the one poin-t that my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Fowler) has taken objection to; I am not wedded to the form of this section. If my hon. friend wants to make any other provisions than that a man must be 21 years of age and a British subject, I have no objection so long as it does not involve the question of preliminary objections.

He may be the biggest
blackleg in the world.

That may be true, but
if he is a British subject and 21 years of age he is entitled to vote.
Suppose there were preliminary objections, but no appeal.

The .preliminary objections wouild take up months and months of time if there were no 'appeals. The moment you bring in the principle of preliminary objections you are defeating the object of this Bill. I do not care what .amendments you have so long as they do not adopt the principle of preliminary objections.

May I sug-
[DOT] gest that as it is nearly 12 o'clock it is pretty far advanced to take up the discussion of such an important measure as this. We had better sleep over it, and then when we come again to stuay the Bill we shall perhaps be in a better frame of mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
agree to the suggestion of my right hon. friend. I think we have gained a great deal by this expression of opifiiori from both sides of the House. But before moving that the committee rise I should like to point out one thing, and that is this. It is required that the man shall be upon the list. Now the fact that he is upon the list shows that the question of his qualification has been tried out once and determined by whatever machinery is provided in the different provinces for ascertatining whether a man ought to be on the list or not.
In my province we have no voters' lists.

Tnat is provided
for.

All that is required
is an affidavit. A man who was irresponsible could put up $1,000 and the cost of the trial might amount to $5,000 or $6,000.

Perhaps the minister does not understand how the voters' lists are made up in some of the provinces. In the province of New Brunswick there is no contest whatever in many cases. Names are put down on the list of men who may be disqualified by reason of non-residence, non-age, or something else. Of course there are contests in some districts of New Brunswick, but the practice varies in different provinces. But because a man's name is on the voters' list, it does not necessarily follow that the matter has been tried by some tribunal. His name may have been placed on the list simply because he happens to be on the assessment list, and without any trial whatever. It seems to me that the consideration that should apply is that, before a man can challenge the election of any man who has been ohosen as the representative of qualified voters, he should himself be of that class. It seems to me that is a reasonable proposition. I shall probably not be here when the Bill comes up again, but I appeal to the sense of this committee to insist that the man shall be a qualified voter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What I was proceeding to point out was that the fact that a man was on the list shows that at some time it had been decided by somebody, however imperfect the machinery-I do not wish to discuss that-that he was a qualified voter. Under the provisions of the Act he is on the list. That entitles him to vote. He may

be called upon to swear that he wa3 not bribed and so forth, but as to his qualification to be a voter he is, as I understand the Act, on the list and qualified to vote.
Could he not be called upon to swear that he was a British subject and a qualified voter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If the hon. member will allow me, I did not intend to conclude bysaying that he is entirely wrong, or by saying that what he says should not perhaps be acted upon. I was just pointing out that the fact that he is on the list shows this much, -that by such machinery as the different provincial legislatures thought was sufficient-and we are proceeding on the basis that we are willing to accept that as our present system of regulating our franchise-that man has been found to be a qualified voter. Now what we propose to do is to take that a step further. It is suggested that manj awfully	evil	things will follow
from it. The hon. gentleman says that an irresponsible person may make a petition. That is absolutely true. But I wonder how many of us have ever come across an election petitioner who was a responsible person! I should be glad to meet any hon. member who has met such a one, because he had an exceptional experience, I think.
I have known very many responsible petitioners in the province of New Brunswick.
And so have T. Some of them are candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It has not been my experience. Those that I have had occasion to come in contact with were so highly irresponsible that they seemed to me to be invisible. I never was able to get in touch with them.
There are a few like that in the province of New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
At all events it is perfectly possible to happen, and I do know that it does happen in some cases. So that after all the evil may not be so terribly serious. Technically, of course, it looks a very awful thing that a man who is not a voter may make a petition. It is said that blacklegs and scallawags may make a petition. Unfortunately blacklegs and scallawags may vote. Unfortunately there are such people on the voters' lists. I am

quite prepared to give consideration to what has been said. I am always prepared to do that. If the hon. gentleman had said that we should have prima facie proof and not conclusive proof, always provided that by that we do not open the door to any preliminary trial on the subject of the man's qualifications, I should be perfectly willing to consider that. That is what we want to get at. It is not so very material whether you have conclusive proof or not, provided you do not interfere with this provision of the Bill that there shall be only one trial, and you will try everything at that trial. So long as we stand to that, I do not know that it is very material whether at that trial you allow the respondent, if he wants to, to start in to prove that that man who was on the list was not qualified. But we must have no two trials. There must be no issue to be separately tried, on the question whether or not the petitioner is qualified. That issue, if there is to be such must be fried simultaneously with the merits of the petition. There must be but one trial, that trial should go on as speedily possible. If we can secure that, for my part I shall be satisfied, and I fancy that any colleagues upon the committee will be satisfied too. I am quite prepared to consider whether making it prima facie proof would not do just as well as making it conclusive proof, as long as whatever the defendant wants to say on qualification is heard at the same time as anything else he wants to say in answer to it.
Or that he may be twenty-one years of age and a British subject.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. Now, I am quite prepared to accept the suggestion of my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). Perhaps we will be better able to deal with this measure after we have slept over it, and therefore I beg to move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
